L117@P3: Rationale: This rule supports a basic principle of data-hiding. Clearly if an object is
L118@P3: not in scope, its value cannot be referenced or corrupted. Similarly, if an erroneous
L119@P3: value of an object has to be diagnosed, the fewer the number of statements where the
L120@P3: value could have been assigned; the easier it is to diagnose the problem. The rule
L121@P3: discourages the re-use of variables for multiple, incompatible purposes, which can
L122@P3: complicate fault diagnosis.

L124@P3: function, and the validity of parameters must be checked inside each function.
L125@P3: Rationale: This is possibly the most frequently violated rule, and therefore somewhat
L126@P3: more suspect as a general rule. In its strictest form, this rule means that even the
L127@P3: return value of printf statements and file close statements must be checked. One can
L128@P3: make a case, though, that if the response to an error would rightfully be no different
L129@P3: than the response to success, there is little point in explicitly checking a return value.

L131@P3: acceptable to explicitly cast the function return value to (void) – thereby indicating
L132@P3: that the programmer explicitly and not accidentally decides to ignore a return value.

L134@P3: irrelevant. In most cases, though, the return value of a function should not be ignored,

L137@P3: for instance, what happens if you accidentally execute strlen(0), or strcat(s1, s2, -1)

L139@P3: make sure that exceptions must be justified, with mechanical checkers flagging
L140@P3: violations. Often, it will be easier to comply with the rule than to explain why noncompliance might be acceptable.
L141@P3: 8. Rule: The use of the preprocessor must be limited to the inclusion of header files and
L142@P3: simple macro definitions. Token pasting, variable argument lists (ellipses), and
L143@P3: recursive macro calls are not allowed. All macros must expand into complete

L146@P3: more than one or two conditional compilation directives even in large software
L147@P3: development efforts, beyond the standard boilerplate that avoids multiple inclusion of
L148@P3: the same header file. Each such use should be flagged by a tool-based checker and
L149@P3: justified in the code.
L150@P3: Rationale: The C preprocessor is a powerful obfuscation tool that can destroy code
L151@P3: clarity and befuddle many text based checkers. The effect of constructs in unrestricted
L152@P3-4: preprocessor code can be extremely hard to decipher, even with a formal language definition in hand. In a new implementation of the C preprocessor, developers often

L154@P4: defining language in the C standard. The rationale for the caution against conditional
L155@P4: compilation is equally important. Note that with just ten conditional compilation
L156@P4: directives, there could be up to 210 possible versions of the code, each of which would
L157@P4: have to be tested– causing a huge increase in the required test effort.
L158@P4: 9. Rule: The use of pointers should be restricted. Specifically, no more than one level of
L159@P4: dereferencing is allowed. Pointer dereference operations may not be hidden in macro
L160@P4: definitions or inside typedef declarations. Function pointers are not permitted.
L161@P4: Rationale: Pointers are easily misused, even by experienced programmers. They can
L162@P4: make it hard to follow or analyze the flow of data in a program, especially by toolbased static analyzers. Function pointers, similarly, can seriously restrict the types of
L163@P4: checks that can be performed by static analyzers and should only be used if there is a
L164@P4: strong justification for their use, and ideally alternate means are provided to assist
L165@P4: tool-based checkers determine flow of control and function call hierarchies. For
L166@P4: instance, if function pointers are used, it can become impossible for a tool to prove
L167@P4: absence of recursion, so alternate guarantees would have to be provided to make up
L168@P4: for this loss in analytical capabilities.
L169@P4: 10. Rule: All code must be compiled, from the first day of development, with all
L170@P4: compiler warnings enabled at the compiler’s most pedantic setting. All code must
L171@P4: compile with these setting without any warnings. All code must be checked daily with
L172@P4: at least one, but preferably more than one, state-of-the-art static source code analyzer
L173@P4: and should pass the analyses with zero warnings.
L174@P4: Rationale: There are several very effective static source code analyzers on the
L175@P4: market today, and quite a few freeware tools as well.2 There simply is no excuse for
L176@P4: any software development effort not to make use of this readily available technology.
L177@P4: It should be considered routine practice, even for non-critical code development.
L178@P4: The rule of zero warnings applies even in cases where the compiler or the static
L179@P4: analyzer gives an erroneous warning: if the compiler or the static analyzer gets
L180@P4: confused, the code causing the confusion should be rewritten so that it becomes more
L181@P4: trivially valid. Many developers have been caught in the assumption that a warning
L182@P4: was surely invalid, only to realize much later that the message was in fact valid for
L183@P4: less obvious reasons. Static analyzers have somewhat of a bad reputation due to early
L184@P4: predecessors, such as lint, that produced mostly invalid messages, but this is no

L186@P4: and accurate messages. Their use should not be negotiable at any serious software
L187@P4: project.
L188@P4: The first two rules guarantee the creation of a clear and transparent control flow structure
L189@P4: that is easier to build, test, and analyze. The absence of dynamic memory allocation,
L190@P4-5: 2 For an overview see, for instance, http://spinroot.com/static/index.htmlstipulated by the third rule, eliminates a class of problems related to the allocation and
L191@P5: freeing of memory, the use of stray pointers, etc. The next few rules (4 to 7) are fairly
L192@P5: broadly accepted as standards for good coding style. Some benefits of other coding styles
L193@P5: that have been advanced for safety critical systems, e.g., the discipline of “design by
L194@P5: contract” can partly be found in rules 5 to 7.

## HEAD (no branch)
./AGENTS.md
# nexus-code agent guide

TypeScript CLI (`cli/`), Rust core (`core/`), eval harness (`eval/`). Current plans: `docs/v1.2.1/PLAN.md`, then `docs/v1.3.0/PLAN.md`. Per-release records live in `docs/releases/` and `docs/evidence/`.

## Build and test
- Build: `make build` (core, then `tsc` in `cli/`). Everything: `make test`; the CI-equivalent run: `make test-ci`. Lint the core with `cargo clippy`; `cli/` has no lint script, `npm --prefix cli run build` type-checks it.
- One TypeScript test file: `cd cli && HOME=$(mktemp -d) node --import tsx --test test/<name>.test.ts`. A throwaway `HOME` is mandatory: a test that touched the real `HOME` once overwrote `~/.config/nexus/config.env`.
- Done = the affected test files pass, plus `tsc` for TypeScript changes. CI is the arbiter; a failure that appears only locally comes from host state first (an unbuilt `cli/dist` or Rust core, a stray `/tmp/.git`), so rule that out before calling it a defect.
- Test-runner or process-handling changes run on Node 22 and 24: the two emit different `node:test` events.
- Rust builds use an isolated `CARGO_TARGET_DIR` per worktree.
- Preserve existing comments and unrelated changes.
- Entire CLI: export `ENTIRE_TOKEN_STORE=file` before any `entire` command. The Entire gate no longer counts toward merging.

## Reference coding with XERJ (required)
- Before writing non-trivial code that has a peer-project analogue (feature, protocol, parser, worktree or provider handling, tool, test harness), read what mature projects do: query the local XERJ node, then record what you took, borrowed or rejected in the PR's "Reference coding" section. Exempt: trivial edits, doc-only changes, fixes fully specified by a failing test.
- Node, commands, corpora, licence and privacy rules, the field report, and the fallback when XERJ is unavailable ("XERJ unavailable: <reason>" plus `git grep`): `docs/XERJ_REFERENCE_CODING.md`. Read it when you start that first query.

## Concurrency, claims and release authority
- Several agents can work here: follow `docs/v1.0.0/CONCURRENCY.md`. Claim a slice or hot file under `$(git rev-parse --git-common-dir)/nexus-claims/` before editing; one worktree and branch per slice (`~/nexus-wt/`), never `~/nexus-code` itself; isolate `HOME` for every test or probe; stop a process by its own pid, never `pkill -f`; check `git log` for foreign commits before each commit.
- Take the `GATEWAY` claim for any inference run; the key comes from the environment (`~/.config/nexus/config.env`) and is never printed. The gateway is the only live provider.
- Push, tag and publish only on an explicit owner instruction; release authority is the owner's.

## Merging and releasing
Bias to correct: a green PR is not a green `main`, and a pushed tag cannot be taken back.
- When merging: required checks are `test-matrix (22)`, `test-matrix (24)`, `linux-x86_64`; read each check's conclusion (empty or in-progress is not success). Merge with a merge commit, `gh pr merge <n> --merge --match-head-commit <full-sha>`. PRs that touch one subsystem merge one at a time, each followed by the CI run on `main`: two PRs green alone can break `main` together.
- When a PR's checks look wrong after `main` moved: PR checks run on GitHub's merge commit, so confirm the run checked out the current `merge_commit_sha` (`gh api repos/<owner>/<repo>/pulls/<n> --jq .merge_commit_sha`); a stale one tests old content.
- When cutting a stable release: make a version-only commit directly on the accepted RC (`node scripts/check-version-only-diff.mjs <rc-ref> <stable-ref>`), land it on `main` through a merge-commit PR, and only then tag, because `release.yml` requires the tagged commit to be an ancestor of `main`. Version tags are immutable: re-run a failed run, or move to the next RC or patch. Then follow `docs/RELEASE_PROCESS.md`.
- When reporting a gate or a result: state it as measured ("ledger closed, qualification pending"), record failed runs unaltered, and make no frontier-grade claim without external qualification.
- Before tagging or merging, check: required checks green at the exact head? CI on `main` green after the previous merge? Tagged commit an ancestor of `main`? Claims match the evidence?

--- toolchain ---
[toolchain]
channel = "1.95.0"
components = ["rustfmt", "clippy"]
profile = "minimal"

--- tests scripts ---
// Runs the CLI test suite with a throwaway HOME so no test (or anything it spawns: the sidecar, the TUI, PTY drivers)
// can read or write the operator's ~/.nexus or ~/.config/nexus. The real home is passed as NEXUS_TEST_REAL_HOME so the
// guard test can prove the isolation held. Arguments are test files; none means every test/*.test.ts.
// NEXUS_KEEP_TEST_HOME=1 keeps the temporary home for inspection.
// One node:test run (run_tests_driver.mjs, in its own process group, files one at a time as before) with a per-file
// watchdog: a file still running after NEXUS_TEST_FILE_TIMEOUT_SECS (default 300) is named with its last output, the
// whole group is killed, and the run restarts with the remaining files so every other failure is still reported.
import { spawn } from "node:child_process";
import fs from "node:fs";
import os from "node:os";
import path from "node:path";
import { fileURLToPath } from "node:url";

const cli = path.resolve(path.dirname(fileURLToPath(import.meta.url)), "..");
const realHome = os.homedir();
const home = fs.mkdtempSync(path.join(os.tmpdir(), "nexus-test-home-"));

const files = process.argv.length > 2
  ? process.argv.slice(2)
  : [
      ...fs.readdirSync(path.join(cli, "test")).filter((f) => f.endsWith(".test.ts")).sort().map((f) => path.join("test", f)),
      path.resolve(cli, "../eval/dataset.test.mjs"),
      path.resolve(cli, "../eval/package_runtime.test.mjs"),
    ];

const env = {
  ...process.env,
  HOME: home,
  XDG_CONFIG_HOME: path.join(home, ".config"),
  XDG_DATA_HOME: path.join(home, ".local", "share"),
  XDG_STATE_HOME: path.join(home, ".local", "state"),
  XDG_CACHE_HOME: path.join(home, ".cache"),
  NEXUS_TEST_REAL_HOME: realHome,
};
// Rust and Node toolchains installed per user keep working under the throwaway home.
for (const [key, dir] of [["CARGO_HOME", ".cargo"], ["RUSTUP_HOME", ".rustup"]]) {
  if (!env[key] && fs.existsSync(path.join(realHome, dir))) env[key] = path.join(realHome, dir);
}

const timeoutSecs = Number(process.env.NEXUS_TEST_FILE_TIMEOUT_SECS) > 0 ? Number(process.env.NEXUS_TEST_FILE_TIMEOUT_SECS) : 300;
const driver = path.join(cli, "scripts", "run_tests_driver.mjs");
let current = null;

function killGroup(child) {
  try { process.kill(-child.pid, "SIGKILL"); } catch { try { child.kill("SIGKILL"); } catch {} }
}

function cleanupHome() {
  if (process.env.NEXUS_KEEP_TEST_HOME === "1") console.error(`test home kept at ${home}`);
  else fs.rmSync(home, { recursive: true, force: true });
}

for (const signal of ["SIGINT", "SIGTERM"]) {
  process.on(signal, () => {
    if (current) killGroup(current);
    cleanupHome();
    process.exit(1);
  });
}

function runSegment(segment) {
  return new Promise((resolve) => {
    const child = spawn(process.execPath, [driver, ...segment], { cwd: cli, env, detached: true, stdio: ["inherit", "inherit", "inherit", "pipe"] });
    current = child;
    const result = { timedOut: undefined, done: undefined };
    let buffered = "";
    child.stdio[3].on("data", (chunk) => {
      buffered += chunk.toString();
      const lines = buffered.split("\n");
      buffered = lines.pop() ?? "";
      for (const line of lines.filter(Boolean)) {
        const message = JSON.parse(line);
        if (message.done) result.done = message;
        if (message.timeout && !result.timedOut) {
          result.timedOut = message.timeout;
          console.error(`\nTEST FILE TIMEOUT after ${timeoutSecs}s: ${message.timeout}\nlast output:\n${message.tail.map((l) => `  | ${l}`).join("\n")}`);
          killGroup(child);
        }
      }
    });
    child.on("error", () => resolve(result));
    child.on("close", () => { killGroup(child); resolve(result); });
  });
}

let remaining = files;
let tests = 0;
let failures = 0;
const timedOut = [];
let crashed = false;
while (remaining.length) {
  const result = await runSegment(remaining);
  if (result.done) {
    tests += result.done.tests;
    failures += result.done.fail;
    break;
  }
  if (!result.timedOut) { crashed = true; break; }
  timedOut.push(result.timedOut);
  const at = remaining.findIndex((f) => path.resolve(cli, f) === result.timedOut);
  remaining = at < 0 ? [] : remaining.slice(at + 1);
}

cleanupHome();
const bad = failures > 0 || timedOut.length > 0 || crashed;

# nexus-code agent guide

TypeScript CLI (`cli/`), Rust core (`core/`), eval harness (`eval/`). Current plans: `docs/v1.2.1/PLAN.md`, then `docs/v1.3.0/PLAN.md`. Per-release records live in `docs/releases/` and `docs/evidence/`.

## Build and test
- Build: `make build` (core, then `tsc` in `cli/`). Everything: `make test`; the CI-equivalent run: `make test-ci`. Lint the core with `cargo clippy`; `cli/` has no lint script, `npm --prefix cli run build` type-checks it.
- One TypeScript test file: `cd cli && HOME=$(mktemp -d) node --import tsx --test test/<name>.test.ts`. A throwaway `HOME` is mandatory: a test that touched the real `HOME` once overwrote `~/.config/nexus/config.env`.
- Done = the affected test files pass, plus `tsc` for TypeScript changes. CI is the arbiter; a failure that appears only locally comes from host state first (an unbuilt `cli/dist` or Rust core, a stray `/tmp/.git`), so rule that out before calling it a defect.
- Test-runner or process-handling changes run on Node 22 and 24: the two emit different `node:test` events.
- Rust builds use an isolated `CARGO_TARGET_DIR` per worktree.
- Preserve existing comments and unrelated changes.
- Entire CLI: export `ENTIRE_TOKEN_STORE=file` before any `entire` command. The Entire gate no longer counts toward merging.

## Reference coding with XERJ (required)
- Before writing non-trivial code that has a peer-project analogue (feature, protocol, parser, worktree or provider handling, tool, test harness), read what mature projects do: query the local XERJ node, then record what you took, borrowed or rejected in the PR's "Reference coding" section. Exempt: trivial edits, doc-only changes, fixes fully specified by a failing test.
- Node, commands, corpora, licence and privacy rules, the field report, and the fallback when XERJ is unavailable ("XERJ unavailable: <reason>" plus `git grep`): `docs/XERJ_REFERENCE_CODING.md`. Read it when you start that first query.

## Concurrency, claims and release authority
- Several agents can work here: follow `docs/v1.0.0/CONCURRENCY.md`. Claim a slice or hot file under `$(git rev-parse --git-common-dir)/nexus-claims/` before editing; one worktree and branch per slice (`~/nexus-wt/`), never `~/nexus-code` itself; isolate `HOME` for every test or probe; stop a process by its own pid, never `pkill -f`; check `git log` for foreign commits before each commit.
- Take the `GATEWAY` claim for any inference run; the key comes from the environment (`~/.config/nexus/config.env`) and is never printed. The gateway is the only live provider.
- Push, tag and publish only on an explicit owner instruction; release authority is the owner's.

## Merging and releasing
Bias to correct: a green PR is not a green `main`, and a pushed tag cannot be taken back.
- When merging: required checks are `test-matrix (22)`, `test-matrix (24)`, `linux-x86_64`; read each check's conclusion (empty or in-progress is not success). Merge with a merge commit, `gh pr merge <n> --merge --match-head-commit <full-sha>`. PRs that touch one subsystem merge one at a time, each followed by the CI run on `main`: two PRs green alone can break `main` together.
- When a PR's checks look wrong after `main` moved: PR checks run on GitHub's merge commit, so confirm the run checked out the current `merge_commit_sha` (`gh api repos/<owner>/<repo>/pulls/<n> --jq .merge_commit_sha`); a stale one tests old content.
- When cutting a stable release: make a version-only commit directly on the accepted RC (`node scripts/check-version-only-diff.mjs <rc-ref> <stable-ref>`), land it on `main` through a merge-commit PR, and only then tag, because `release.yml` requires the tagged commit to be an ancestor of `main`. Version tags are immutable: re-run a failed run, or move to the next RC or patch. Then follow `docs/RELEASE_PROCESS.md`.
- When reporting a gate or a result: state it as measured ("ledger closed, qualification pending"), record failed runs unaltered, and make no frontier-grade claim without external qualification.
- Before tagging or merging, check: required checks green at the exact head? CI on `main` green after the previous merge? Tagged commit an ancestor of `main`? Claims match the evidence?

import path from "node:path";

  XDG_DATA_HOME: path.join(home, ".local", "share"),
  XDG_STATE_HOME: path.join(home, ".local", "state"),

}

for (const signal of ["SIGINT", "SIGTERM"]) {
  process.on(signal, () => {
    if (current) killGroup(current);
    cleanupHome();
    process.exit(1);
  });
}

function runSegment(segment) {
  return new Promise((resolve) => {
    const child = spawn(process.execPath, [driver, ...segment], { cwd: cli, env, detached: true, stdio: ["inherit", "inherit", "inherit", "pipe"] });
    current = child;
    const result = { timedOut: undefined, done: undefined };
    let buffered = "";
    child.stdio[3].on("data", (chunk) => {
      buffered += chunk.toString();
      const lines = buffered.split("\n");
      buffered = lines.pop() ?? "";
      for (const line of lines.filter(Boolean)) {
        const message = JSON.parse(line);
        if (message.done) result.done = message;
        if (message.timeout && !result.timedOut) {
          result.timedOut = message.timeout;
          console.error(`\nTEST FILE TIMEOUT after ${timeoutSecs}s: ${message.timeout}\nlast output:\n${message.tail.map((l) => `  | ${l}`).join("\n")}`);
          killGroup(child);
        }
      }
    });
    child.on("error", () => resolve(result));
    child.on("close", () => { killGroup(child); resolve(result); });
  });
}

let remaining = files;
let tests = 0;
let failures = 0;
const timedOut = [];
let crashed = false;
while (remaining.length) {
  const result = await runSegment(remaining);
  if (result.done) {
    tests += result.done.tests;
    failures += result.done.fail;
    break;
  }
  if (!result.timedOut) { crashed = true; break; }
  timedOut.push(result.timedOut);
  const at = remaining.findIndex((f) => path.resolve(cli, f) === result.timedOut);
  remaining = at < 0 ? [] : remaining.slice(at + 1);
}

cleanupHome();
const bad = failures > 0 || timedOut.length > 0 || crashed;
if (timedOut.length || crashed) console.error(`\ntimed out: ${timedOut.join(", ") || "none"}${crashed ? "; the test driver exited without a result" : ""}; tests (completed segments): ${tests}, fail: ${failures}`);
process.exit(bad ? 1 : 0);

export PATH := $(HOME)/.cargo/bin:$(PATH)
APPROVED_RUST_BUILD_IMAGE := rust:1.95.0-bookworm@sha256:4c2fd73ef19c5ef9d54bee03b06b2839a392604fbfcd578ed948b71b37c1d7fb

.PHONY: all setup build build-core build-cli check clean test test-ci test-fixture-notice audit security-scan sbom verify-reproducibility

all: build

setup:
	npm --prefix cli install
	cargo build --release --manifest-path core/Cargo.toml
	npm --prefix cli run build

build: build-core build-cli

build-core:
	cargo build --release --manifest-path core/Cargo.toml

build-cli:
	npm --prefix cli run build

check:
	node cli/dist/index.js check

clean:
	cargo clean --manifest-path core/Cargo.toml
	rm -rf dist cli/dist cli/node_modules

audit:
	npm --prefix cli audit

security-scan:
	bash scripts/security_gates.sh

sbom:
	bash scripts/generate_sbom.sh

verify-reproducibility:
	@echo "[*] Verifying reproducible package build..."
	@TMP1=$$(mktemp -d) && TMP2=$$(mktemp -d) && \
	VERSION=$$(node -p 'require("./package.json").version') && \
	NEXUS_BUILD_CONTAINER_IMAGE=$(APPROVED_RUST_BUILD_IMAGE) bash scripts/package-linux.sh "v$$VERSION" "$$TMP1" && \
	NEXUS_BUILD_CONTAINER_IMAGE=$(APPROVED_RUST_BUILD_IMAGE) bash scripts/package-linux.sh "v$$VERSION" "$$TMP2" && \
	cmp "$$TMP1/nexus-linux-x86_64-v$$VERSION.tar.gz" "$$TMP2/nexus-linux-x86_64-v$$VERSION.tar.gz" && \
	cmp "$$TMP1/SHA256SUMS" "$$TMP2/SHA256SUMS" && \
	cmp "$$TMP1/THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.txt" "$$TMP2/THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.txt" && \
	cmp "$$TMP1/sbom.cdx.json" "$$TMP2/sbom.cdx.json" && \
	cmp "$$TMP1/install.sh" "$$TMP2/install.sh" && \
	rm -rf "$$TMP1" "$$TMP2"
	@echo "[+] Reproducible build verification succeeded (byte-identical artifacts)."

# `make test` runs every gate and fails at the end, so a CLI failure does not hide the terminal-scope or
# security result. It calls the two halves of `npm --prefix cli test` by name (test:cli, test:scope), so the
# step list lives only in cli/package.json.
# CI evaluator fixtures (tmpfs workspace and runtime root) come from `make test-ci`; see docs/DEVELOPMENT.md.
test: test-fixture-notice
	@rc=0; \
	cargo test --manifest-path core/Cargo.toml || { echo "[!] FAILED: cargo test"; rc=1; }; \
	npm --prefix cli run test:cli || { echo "[!] FAILED: CLI suite"; rc=1; }; \
	npm --prefix cli run test:scope || { echo "[!] FAILED: terminal scope"; rc=1; }; \
	bash scripts/security_gates.sh || { echo "[!] FAILED: security gates"; rc=1; }; \
	if [ $$rc -ne 0 ]; then echo "[!] make test: one or more steps failed (all steps ran)"; fi; \
	exit $$rc

test-fixture-notice:
	@if [ -z "$$NEXUS_EVAL_TEST_WORKSPACE_ROOT" ] || [ -z "$$NEXUS_EVAL_TEST_RUNTIME_ROOT" ]; then \
	  echo "[i] NEXUS_EVAL_TEST_WORKSPACE_ROOT / NEXUS_EVAL_TEST_RUNTIME_ROOT are not set."; \
	  echo "[i] cli/test/eval_version_probe_storage.test.ts will FAIL without them, and cli/test/eval_integrity.test.ts"; \
	  echo "[i] runs its /dev/shm fallback branches instead of the capped-tmpfs ones. This is not a code defect."; \
	  echo "[i] Run 'make test-ci' to provision the same fixtures as CI (needs sudo)."; \
	fi

# Same gates as CI with the CI evaluator fixtures: mounts a capped tmpfs and runtime root, runs `make test`,
# then unmounts and removes only what it created. One-time host setup (not run here):
# scripts/install-evaluator-toolchains.sh, scripts/ensure-ci-bubblewrap.sh, scripts/ensure-ci-user-cgroups.sh.
test-ci:
	+@if [ -n "$(findstring n,$(firstword -$(MAKEFLAGS)))" ]; then echo 'dry run: would run scripts/with-ci-fixtures.sh -- make test'; else bash scripts/with-ci-fixtures.sh -- $(MAKE) test; fi

The CLI and the TUI sidecar run as child processes with an isolated HOME against a mock provider answering 429 + Retry-After; nothing writes state directly. Residual: lines pasted into a file that already existed (status M) are never line-compared; a commented-out secret line is not matched; in the plain diff for a subdirectory workspace the protected-source listings are relative to that subdirectory; `.nexus` links and files over the bound are left out by design; the snapshot does not run the comparison. # Nexus Code Architecture

Nexus Code utilizes a split architecture designed for performance, modularity, and security:

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                 TypeScript Orchestration Layer              │
│   • REPL / TUI Interface        • Agent Intelligence        │
│   • Skills Engine               • MCP JSON-RPC Client       │
│   • Plugin Lifecycle System     • Checkpoint & Undo Engine  │
│   • Secret Redactor             • Session Persistence       │
└──────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────┘
                               │ IPC / CLI Subprocess
┌──────────────────────────────▼──────────────────────────────┐
│                    Rust Core Engine (ELF)                   │
│   • Path Resolution Jail        • Ripgrep Fast Search       │
│   • Atomic File Ops             • AST Symbol Parser         │
│   • Patch / Diff Applicator     • Tree & Metadata Inspector │
│   • POSIX Command Runner        • Destructive Command Guard │
└──────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────┘
                               │ HTTP / SSE Gateway
┌──────────────────────────────▼──────────────────────────────┐
│          OpenAI-compatible inference endpoint               │
│   • Local server: llama.cpp, vLLM, LM Studio, Ollama        │
│   • Optional gateway or cloud provider (operator-selected)  │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

---

## 1. Rust Core Engine (`core/`)

The core engine is implemented in Rust 2024 edition and compiled into an optimized 64-bit ELF binary (`harness-core`).
- **`file_ops.rs`**: Safe reading with 8 MB cap and paging hints (`offset`, `length`), writing, atomic replacement, metadata inspection (`file_info`), batch reading (`batch_read` with 8 MB cap per entry), unified patch application (`patch_file`), and path traversal prevention (`resolve_safe_path`).
- **`search.rs`**: Fast ripgrep search using `ignore` and `grep` crates, regex symbol extraction across multi-language ASTs, and Unicode file tree formatting (`file_tree`).
- **`runner.rs`**: Child process execution and process ownership tracking via `ProcessRegistry`. Tracks process group IDs (`pgid`) mapped to request IDs. ## 3. Controls and their limits

Each control below is stated with what it does **not** cover. The v1.0.0 plan (`docs/v1.0.0/`) tracks the open gaps.

1. **Workspace path jail (file tools).** The Rust file tools (read, write, edit, delete, list, search) canonicalize every path against the workspace root and reject `..`, absolute paths and symlink escapes, rechecking the opened descriptor. *Limit:* for `run_command`, path protection is advisory. Host commands have the user's filesystem access unless the sandbox (`--sandbox`) or read-only HOME masking (`--read-only` with `bwrap`) is enabled.
2. **Destructive-command tripwire.** Shell-words tokenization in TypeScript (`cli/src/security.ts`) and Rust (`core/src/runner.rs`) stops obviously destructive commands (`rm -rf /`, `mkfs`, raw block device writes, fork bombs) without false positives on legitimate project commands (`rm -rf ./build`, `rm -rf /tmp/x`, `grep reboot`, `echo shutdown`, `chown -R me /srv`). *Limit:* this is explicitly a convenience tripwire to catch obvious mistakes, **not** a security boundary. Alternative invocations (`find / -delete`, `/bin/rm -rf /`, `rm -r -f /`, Python scripts) are documented non-goals that pass through by design. The sandbox (`--sandbox`) and approval posture (`review`) form the security boundary.
3. **Approvals and posture defaults.** Per amended DEC-01, unset permission mode defaults to `review` regardless of folder trust. `--mode auto` permits writes and commands while retaining first-use egress approval per origin; `--yes` and `NEXUS_APPROVAL_MODE=auto` enable full access and bypass approval prompts, including egress. Folder trust only controls project instructions and workspace integrations. Input safety is strictly enforced across surfaces (REQ-SEC-103): lone Enter defaults to No, a 400ms grace period discards typed-ahead input, and approve-all requires explicit confirmation (`all` in REPL, confirmation Enter in TUI). *Limit:* in explicit `auto` posture, commands and file writes execute autonomously regardless of folder trust. Egress approval covers the network tools (`fetch_web`, `search_web` and the `browser_*` tools, classed `egress`); it does **not** cover shell commands. `run_command` is classed `exec`, so a shell command such as `curl` or `git push` is never checked against the egress origin list, and the only thing that confines its network access is the network setting of `--sandbox` (item 6). In `review` mode the operator sees the command and approves it as a whole; with `--sandbox` the approval prompt also states whether the sandbox has network access.
4. **Workspace trust.** Trust is managed via `nexus trust` and stored in `~/.config/nexus/trusted_workspaces.json`; interactive startup asks for trust before loading project instructions (`AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md`, `CODEX.md`, `.nexusrules`). In untrusted workspaces, project instructions, workspace MCP configs, plugins, skills, and `.nexus/knowledge.json` are not loaded (REQ-SEC-113, REQ-SEC-114). The operator may continue without trust under the existing permission mode or exit. *Limit:* configuration in the operator's home directory (`~/.config/nexus/`, `~/.nexus/`) is always trusted.
5. **Secret redaction.** Terminal output, audit logs and durable state pass through pattern-based scrubbers, and outbound content is classified and tokenized. *Limit:* it is pattern-based, so secrets with no recognizable shape are not detected.
6. **Container sandbox and argv isolation.** `--sandbox` confines execution using Linux Bubblewrap (`bwrap`) or Docker. The sandbox argv is constructed as a direct array without shell wrapping (REQ-SEC-109), preventing shell escaping flaws on complex workspace paths. The write-mode `bwrap` sandbox (`cli/src/sandbox.ts`) is built as follows:
   - *Filesystem:* the host root is bound read-only (`--ro-bind / /`, remounted read-only) with a fresh `/dev`, `/proc` and an empty `/tmp`; the workspace is bound writable. `$HOME` is replaced by an empty tmpfs, so `~/.ssh`, `~/.aws`, `~/.gnupg`, `~/.config/nexus` and browser profiles do not exist inside. Only toolchain directories are bound back read-only: `~/.cargo`, `~/.rustup`, `~/.nvm`, `~/.local/bin`, `~/.npm`, `~/.cache/pip`, `~/go/pkg`, the `PATH` entries that lie under `$HOME` (with their `<prefix>` for a `.../bin` entry), and the paths the operator lists in `NEXUS_SANDBOX_HOME_READONLY` (comma-separated; operator environment or `config.env` only, never a project `.env`). A candidate that is, contains or sits inside a credential location (the same list plus `~/.config`, `~/.local/share`, `~/.cache` as whole directories) is refused, including through a symlink. `~/.cargo/credentials` and `~/.cargo/credentials.toml` are masked with `/dev/null`. `/run/user/<uid>` (ssh/gpg agents, user bus) is an empty tmpfs, and `/run/docker.sock` and `/var/run/docker.sock` are masked. The workspace bind is applied on top of the masked `$HOME`, so when the workspace is `$HOME`, or contains a credential path, those paths are overlaid (a tmpfs for a directory, `/dev/null` for a file) after the workspace bind; they appear empty. `nexus doctor` (`sandbox.confinement`) lists the effective mounts, masks and refusals.
   - *Environment:* `--clearenv`, then only the scrubbed command environment (`cli/src/command_env.ts`) is set. Variables that came from `~/.config/nexus/config.env`, names that look like credentials (`*_API_KEY`, `*_TOKEN`, `*_SECRET`, `*_PASSWORD`, `AWS_*`, `GH_TOKEN`, `SSH_AUTH_SOCK`, ...) and proxy URLs with embedded credentials are removed. The operator can pass a named variable through with `NEXUS_COMMAND_ENV_PASSTHROUGH` (comma-separated, trailing `*` for a prefix; operator environment or `config.env` only, never a project `.env`). The same scrubbed environment applies to `run_command` without `--sandbox`, and the Rust runner (`core/src/runner.rs`) removes credential-looking names again as a second layer.
   - *Network:* off by default (`--unshare-net`; Docker `--network none`). The operator opts in with `--sandbox-network` or `NEXUS_SANDBOX_NETWORK=1` in the operator environment. `--yes` does not enable it. `--sandbox-network` without `--sandbox` has no effect and warns. `--read-only` mode is always offline.
   - *Process isolation:* `--unshare-pid` with a fresh `/proc` (host processes and their `/proc/<pid>/environ` are invisible) and `--die-with-parent` (every descendant dies with the runner). These flags are on both the write-mode and the read-only `bwrap` branches. `--new-session` is deliberately not used: it makes `bwrap` its own session leader, so the runner's `killpg` on cancel or deadline no longer reached the sandbox. Keystroke injection into the operator's terminal (TIOCSTI) is closed by the kernel default `legacy_tiocsti=0` (Linux 6.2 and later), not by the sandbox.
   - *Docker:* the image is pinned by digest in one constant, `DOCKER_SANDBOX_IMAGE` (`alpine:3.23@sha256:469c9ea4...`). The operator may substitute another with `NEXUS_SANDBOX_DOCKER_IMAGE` (operator environment or `config.env`); it must match `name@sha256:<64 hex>`, otherwise no container is started. The container runs with `--user <uid>:<gid>` of the invoking user, `--cap-drop ALL`, `--security-opt no-new-privileges`, `--pids-limit 512`, `--read-only` and `--tmpfs /tmp:rw,nosuid,nodev,size=256m`. The network is `--network none` unless the same opt-in as `bwrap` is set (`--sandbox-network` / `NEXUS_SANDBOX_NETWORK=1`; read-only mode is always offline). Only the scrubbed command environment is passed, one `--env` per variable, with `HOME`, `PATH` and `TMPDIR` replaced by container paths. When the workspace is, contains or sits above `$HOME`, credential paths inside it are overlaid after the workspace mount (`sandboxWorkspaceOverlays`: a tmpfs for a directory, `/dev/null` for a file). Consequence: commands that wrote outside the workspace and `/tmp`, relied on root, or used the network now fail in Docker mode.
   - In `--read-only` mode, `$HOME` is mounted as `--tmpfs $HOME` and the host root is not exposed (REQ-SEC-104); without bwrap, strict path confinement rejects paths outside the workspace.

   *Limits, stated plainly:* (a) **Without `--sandbox`** a command runs as the same user as Nexus. The scrubbed environment keeps credentials out of what the command inherits (`env`, `printenv`), but the command can still read the operator's files (for example `~/.config/nexus/config.env`, `~/.ssh`) and the environment of its parent processes through `/proc/<pid>/environ` (same user; Yama `ptrace_scope=1` does not block that read). Inside the `bwrap` sandbox host processes are invisible. (b) **Under `--sandbox`**, files outside `$HOME` are still readable (`--ro-bind / /`), for example other users' home directories and world-readable system files; only `$HOME` and the locations listed above are masked. (c) The sandbox does not protect against a command the operator approves while the network opt-in is enabled: such a command can send any file it can read to the network. Full container sandboxing requires `bwrap` or Docker on the host.
7. **Process group lifecycle and residual setsid escape risk.** The runner registers child process groups at spawn and terminates entire groups (`killpg`) on turn cancel, client crash, or process shutdown (REQ-AGT-109, REQ-SEC-106). Background services explicitly registered survive turn cancel but are cleaned on client exit. *Limit:* commands that explicitly invoke `setsid()` or create a new session ID escape the process group boundary unless Bubblewrap (`--sandbox`) or Docker isolation is enabled (`bwrap` uses `--die-with-parent` and a PID namespace on both its branches, so all descendants are swept when the runner exits). Documented residual risk: in unsandboxed mode, processes that detach with `setsid()` will outlive cancel sweeps.

## Compaction and continuity

Long-task continuity (no step ceiling, state-aware repetition, objective-scoped execution tracking), the durable
compaction commit, queued operator `/compact`, and optional provider capabilities with labelled token accounting are

# Execution convergence: one lifecycle for autonomous work

Branch `fix/inference-transport-cause`, baseline 9f103ee. Code references are to `cli/src`.

```
user workflow/command (/team [experimental], nexus operation [experimental])
  -> orchestration strategy (TeamOrchestrator: roles -> work units)
  -> durable work units + dependencies (DurableOperationState, OperationStore)
  -> convergence scheduler (ConvergenceScheduler decides; OperationRunner owns time, execution, persistence)
  -> agent turn (AgentWorkUnitExecutor -> runTurn) / provider recovery (ProviderRecoveryController) / context admission
  -> tools + inference resources (ResourceRegistry, LocalLlmClient)
```

Interactive turns (REPL, TUI sidecar, `nexus run`) enter at "agent turn" directly; see section 8.

## 2. The /team false success

Reproduction (`test/team_convergence.test.ts` tests 1–2, failing on 9f103ee): a provider that answers every chat
request with HTTP 400. `/team researcher …` returned `success: true` with the report
`Subagent failed during LLM inference: Inference error (HTTP 400) …`; `/team full …` ran all four roles on the
failed role's missing output and returned success.

Root cause: `TeamOrchestrator.executeRoleTask` built `{ success: true, output: await agent.runSubagent(...) }`, and
`runSubagent` caught inference failure and step-limit exhaustion and *returned* them as the report string. Success
meant "the function returned". `runFullWorkflow` passed each role's text to the next role unconditionally.

## 3. Lifecycle

One model for durable autonomous work, defined in `core/operation.ts` (header) and used by `nexus operation` and
`/team`:

| Unit state | Meaning |
|---|---|
| RUNNABLE | dependencies COMPLETE; waiting for the scheduler |
| RUNNING | a turn is executing on its assigned resource |
| PARKED | a qualified resource will be eligible again at a known time; no model context is held |
| WAITING_ON_DEPENDENCY | some dependency is not COMPLETE (a BLOCKED dependency keeps it here) |
| COMPLETE | the turn completed with an established result: `turnSucceeded(TurnResult)`, the same predicate as `nexus run` exit 0 (outcome `VERIFIED`, or `NOT_REQUIRED`). `UNVERIFIED` work is not complete |
| BLOCKED | no safe autonomous transition; carries one structured decision |

| Operation state | Meaning |
|---|---|
| RUNNING | some unit is runnable or running (the "active" state) |
| WAITING | nothing can run now; required work is parked on a known time |
| BLOCKED | nothing can run or wait; required work needs a decision |
| COMPLETE | every required unit is COMPLETE |
| CANCELLED | the operator stopped it; history preserved |

There is no FAILED state. Terminal execution failure (provider rejection, step limit, unknown execution with its
replay budget spent, interrupted tool, no qualified resource) is BLOCKED with a decision; environmental conditions
(rate limit, capacity, transport outage) park or reroute. `TurnResult` remains the per-turn vocabulary; the unit
state is derived from it in `AgentWorkUnitExecutor.classify`, so no second set of execution enums exists. A turn
that completed without an established result (`UNVERIFIED`: verification not run, no applicable verifier, or
`CONTEXT_EVIDENCE_NOT_RETAINED`) is BLOCKED with a retry/revise decision, never COMPLETE.

`NOT_REQUIRED` means the turn changed nothing *and* every tool output it relied on was still in its context. When
context compaction removes a tool observation (elided or truncated by the detail budget) and the turn does not run
that tool with the same arguments again, the turn is `UNVERIFIED` with reason `CONTEXT_EVIDENCE_NOT_RETAINED`. The
durable record tells the model exactly which outputs left its context (`Output no longer in context (rerun to see it
again): <tool> <args>`), carries which notes still hold full output (`retainedObservations`), and a resumed unit
re-derives what it no longer holds from its recovered conversation. Removal tracking is per turn (plus resumed
conversations); an interactive REPL turn relying on output compacted away in an earlier turn is not flagged.

### Decisions

A BLOCKED unit carries `{ id: "<unit>#<n>", cause, question, options[] }`. Every option is a typed `DecisionAction`:
`retry` (optionally clearing operator-needed resource conditions), `keep_waiting`, `assign` (to a named resource,
listing the requirements it overrides — never independence or trust), `revise` (operator note appended to the unit's
task), `drop` (advisory units only) and `cancel_operation`. `ConvergenceScheduler.resolve` validates the decision id,
the option id and the action against current state and throws `DecisionRejected` otherwise; applying one records
it on `unit.decisions`, emits `DECISION_APPLIED` and resumes the operation under the driver lock. Operators apply
them with `nexus operation decide <operation> <decision> <option> [--note …] [--no-resume]`. Nothing else mutates a
BLOCKED unit.

### Rejected decisions

`nexus operation decide` reports a rejected choice as `Decision rejected: …` on stderr and exits with status `2`.
The rejection happens before the updated operation state is saved, so an invalid choice does not alter durable
operation state. Run `nexus operation status <operation> --json`; the result is a one-element array. Inspect
`$[0].units[].blocked.decision` and `$[0].blocked.decisions` for the current decision IDs, questions, and offered
option IDs. The human-readable status view
shows blocked reasons, but does not list every unit decision's options. Retry with an option ID in the current JSON
state. Do not reuse an option from an older status display: decisions can become stale after another operator action
or after the operation changes state.

The CLI rejects a decision when the operation is already complete or cancelled, the decision ID is no longer
pending, or the option ID is not one currently offered. It also rejects actions that would violate the operation's
contract: `revise` requires `--note`, a required unit cannot be dropped, and `assign` must name a configured resource
that satisfies the unit's minimum trust boundary. Trust requirements cannot be overridden by an operator decision.
For example, inspect the current choices before applying one:

```sh
nexus operation status op-123
nexus operation decide op-123 research#1 2 --note "Use the approved local source"
```

The option number above is illustrative; use the ID shown by `status` for the current operation. The command resumes
the operation after a valid decision unless `--no-resume` is supplied. With `--no-resume`, Nexus records the valid
decision and prints the updated status without starting the operation again.

## 4. /team on the convergence foundation

`TeamOrchestrator` is now a strategy: it maps the request to work units and drives them through `driveOperation`
(the same entry `nexus operation run/resume` uses). `executeRoleTask`, `runFullWorkflow`, `RoleTaskResult` and the
role-specific `runSubagent` prompt plumbing are removed.

| Unit | Role | Depends on | Requirement |
|---|---|---|---|
| research | researcher | — | qualification `research`, capability `tools` |
| design | architect | research | `architecture` |
| implement | implementer | design | `implementation` |
| verify | tester | implement | `verification` |
| review (only with `--independent-review`, or `/team reviewer`) | reviewer | implement | `review`, `independentOf: [implement]` |

`/team <role>` is a one-unit operation. Each unit is an `AgentWorkUnitExecutor` turn (streaming `runTurn` with
provider recovery, context admission and a durable task conversation) run in 15-step segments (with durable checkpoints at segment boundaries; under default continuation units run until completion, stagnation or cancellation, while `--no-continuation` bounds the turn at 15 steps); dependency summaries are
passed to dependents as context. The operation is persisted under `~/.nexus/tasks/team-xxxxxxxx.json`, so
`nexus operation status|resume|decide` work on team operations. `/team` waits in-process up to 60 s; a longer wait
returns `NOT COMPLETE (WAITING)` with the resume command. Ctrl-C in the legacy REPL aborts the operation
(CANCELLED, resumable). The report is derived from operation state: `Result: COMPLETE` only when the operation is
COMPLETE.

Roles are defined once in `core/roles.ts` (`ROLE_PROFILES`, `ROLE_REQUIREMENTS`).

## 5. Capability routing and independence

Resources come from configuration (`resourcesFromConfig`): primary, failover endpoints, and the planner/coder models
when configured. The planner is `preferredFor` research/architecture/review and the coder for
implementation/verification, so roles do not all land on the default model; `ResourceRegistry.select` orders by
preference, then rank. When the chosen resource has a temporary condition the scheduler reroutes to a qualified
eligible alternate; otherwise it parks the unit and continues other eligible work; the operation waits when nothing
can run, and blocks only when no qualified resource exists at all.

`independentOf` is a trust constraint: the review unit can never run on a model that ran `implement`, and `assign`
options never offer a trust-violating resource. If only the implementer's model is available the review parks or
blocks (`NO_QUALIFIED_RESOURCE`); it is never reported as independent.

## 6. Completion propagation

A unit runs only when all of its dependencies are COMPLETE. A BLOCKED dependency leaves its dependents in
WAITING_ON_DEPENDENCY and the operation BLOCKED with the dependency's decision. Advisory units (`required: false`)
are reported but never awaited; `newOperation` rejects a required unit that depends on an advisory one, so advisory
work cannot silently become required.

## 7. Credential boundary

Root cause (9f103ee): `readLatestAuthToken()` read the stored gateway token (`NEXUS_GATEWAY_TOKEN_FILE` / `~/.config/nexus/gateway-token`)
and `LocalLlmClient` attached it to *any* endpoint configured without an explicit key, including failover endpoints
and the 401 reload path; `buildConfig` baked it into `config.apiKey`; planner/coder configs then reused
`config.apiKey` for their own endpoints.

Remediation (no secret-management redesign):

- The stored token and config.env's `LOCAL_LLM_API_KEY` belong to config.env's `LOCAL_LLM_ENDPOINT` origin (else
  `$LOCAL_LLM_ENDPOINT`), plus any origins listed in `LOCAL_LLM_CREDENTIAL_ORIGINS`. `$LOCAL_LLM_API_KEY` belongs to
  `$LOCAL_LLM_ENDPOINT`. An explicit key belongs to `config.credentialOrigin`, else the endpoint it was given for.
- `LocalLlmClient` resolves the credential per request URL (`credentialFor`); a 401 reload re-reads only that
  gateway's stored credential. Endpoints with no credential send `Bearer not-needed`.
- `buildConfig` no longer bakes the stored token into `config.apiKey`; planner/coder configs carry the origin their
  key belongs to; scheduler resources with `apiKeyEnv` get that key scoped to their own endpoint.
- Credential values never appear in operation state, events, reports or errors (test 26 checks all of them).

Origin authority (I6 remediation): only the operator decides where a stored credential may go. `loadEnvironment`
snapshots the process environment before any env file is read and overlays `~/.config/nexus/config.env`; that is
the credential authority (`setCredentialAuthority`). The install `.env` and the working-directory `.env` still
configure endpoints and models, but their `LOCAL_LLM_CREDENTIAL_ORIGINS` / `LOCAL_LLM_ENDPOINT` never widen or
re-home a stored credential (token file, config.env key, or the operator's `LOCAL_LLM_API_KEY`). A key a project
`.env` supplies itself is bound only to that project's endpoint. `mayBindCredential` applies the same rule to a
scheduler resource's `apiKeyEnv`, so a spec cannot point a stored credential at another origin.

## 8. Single-agent boundary

An interactive turn stays a direct `runTurn`: one turn whose `TurnResult` is the outcome, with provider recovery
and context admission inside it. Wrapping it in an operation would add a store and lock but no new truth. Work that
has dependencies, must outlive a resource becoming unavailable, may wait, or must resume after a restart is an
operation. `spawn_subagent` is in-turn delegation: its result is a tool result of the parent's durable turn and is
now truthful (`SubagentResult.completed`; the tool reports `success: false` when the child did not complete). The
child is complete only by `turnSucceeded` on its own turn: its `task_completed` goes through the same receipt
validation as any turn (a rejected receipt keeps it working), and a plain-text report over unverified changes is
not completion. The child's workspace changes count as the parent's, so the parent must verify them before it can
complete; it cannot finish as `NOT_REQUIRED`.

## 9. Restart and reboot

Process restart: proven. Operation state and each unit's task conversation are durable; a driver killed at any
point leaves a lock whose pid is dead, which the next `nexus operation resume` takes over; interrupted RUNNING units
are reconciled (bounded unknown-outcome resumes).

Host reboot: Nexus has no daemon or service lifecycle (the only long-lived child is the per-process Rust RPC
helper), so none was added. After a reboot the state is intact and a lock written before boot is treated as stale
even if its pid number has been reused (`OperationStore.acquire` compares the lock time with boot time). The
smallest integration point is an OS boot hook that runs `nexus operation resume` (with no id it resumes the latest
WAITING or RUNNING operation for the workspace; BLOCKED operations are excluded because they need a decision), e.g.
a user systemd unit or `@reboot

/**
 * Structured turn result (slice: truthful, interruptible turns).
 *
 * Three orthogonal dimensions are reported separately so that no single value has to
 * carry execution, engineering and acceptance meaning at once:
 *
 *   execution   - what happened to the turn itself
 *   outcome     - what Nexus can *demonstrate* about the engineering result
 *   acceptance  - whether an operator accepted the result (never set by Nexus itself)
 *
 * This module is presentation-free: callers (CLI, REPL, a future TUI) project it, they do not
 * reinterpret it. VERIFIED can only be produced from verifier evidence, never asserted.
 */
import type { ToolCallSyntaxCounts } from "../parser.js";
import type { NeedsInputQuestion } from "./needs_input.js";

export type ExecutionState = "COMPLETED" | "INTERRUPTED" | "FAILED" | "BLOCKED" | "LIMIT_REACHED";

/**
 * VERIFIED        - the verifier selected for this workspace ran and passed against the current changes
 * UNVERIFIED      - work ended with a result that was not (or could not be) verified; see reason. Either changes
 *                   no passing verifier covers, or an answer resting on tool output that context compaction removed
 *                   during the turn and the model did not re-read (CONTEXT_EVIDENCE_NOT_RETAINED)
 * NOT_ESTABLISHED - no engineering result was established (turn did not complete, or verifier failed)
 * NOT_REQUIRED    - the turn made no workspace change and every tool output it relied on was still in context
 */
export type EngineeringOutcome = "VERIFIED" | "REGRESSION_FREE" | "UNVERIFIED" | "NOT_ESTABLISHED" | "NOT_REQUIRED";

export type OperatorAcceptance = "NOT_REQUESTED" | "ACCEPTED" | "NOT_ACCEPTED";

export type TurnReason =
  | "NO_APPLICABLE_VERIFIER"
  | "NO_TESTS_EXECUTED"
  | "VERIFICATION_NOT_RUN"
  | "REGRESSION_FREE"
  | "CONTEXT_EVIDENCE_NOT_RETAINED"
  | "VERIFIER_FAILED"
  | "VERIFIER_TIMED_OUT"
  /** The same failure repeated, alternated or grew across fresh candidates: the turn stopped for the operator to decide. */
  | "VERIFIER_NOT_CONVERGING"
  /** The model repeated one tool call with identical arguments and an identical result until the hard threshold. */
  | "TOOL_CALL_LOOP"
  /** A headless run needs an operator decision (approval): BLOCKED with the question in TurnResult.needsInput (VC-9). */
  | "NEEDS_INPUT"
  | "INFERENCE_FAILED"
  | "STEP_LIMIT_REACHED"
  | "STEP_PAUSED"
  /** Continued turn: the total step budget across segments is spent. */
  | "STEP_BUDGET_EXHAUSTED"
  /** Continued turn: the wall-clock budget is spent. */
  | "TIME_BUDGET_EXHAUSTED"
  /** Continued turn: no progress for the configured number of steps, or bounded recovery from a repeated action failed. */
  | "STAGNATION_DETECTED"
  /** The work stopped with operator acceptance requirements still open or blocked (see TurnResult.objective). */
  | "REQUIREMENTS_INCOMPLETE"
  | "OPERATOR_INTERRUPT"
  | "REPOSITORY_STATE_CHANGED"
  | "CONTEXT_CAPACITY_EXCEEDED"
  /** A compaction (or other state the next action depends on) could not be written durably; the turn stopped. */
  | "PERSISTENCE_FAILED"
  | "UNHANDLED_ERROR";

/** What made the model/agent loop stop issuing actions. Not itself evidence of success. */
export type ModelStop = "TASK_COMPLETED_TOOL" | "FINAL_TEXT" | "NONE";

export type InferenceFailureKind =
  | "http_error"
  | "network_error"
  | "timeout"
  | "stream_interrupted"
  | "stream_incomplete"
  | "provider_error_frame"
  | "malformed_event"
  | "output_truncated"
  | "protocol_error"
  | "aborted"
  /** Refused before sending: disclosure not authorized, or a spending limit reached. */
  | "policy_denied"
  /** Refused before sending: the connection lacks a required credential or model. */
  | "configuration_error";

export type InferenceFailureOrigin = "provider" | "transport" | "client" | "operator";

/**
 * What a failed inference request says about the provider. The first four are temporary: the agent loop may wait
 * for them. The rest need a different request, configuration, or the operator.
 */
export type ProviderCondition =
  | "TEMPORARILY_UNAVAILABLE"
  | "RATE_LIMITED"
  | "OVERLOADED"
  | "DRAINING"
  | "AUTH_FAILURE"
  /** Billing or quota exhausted (HTTP 402, insufficient_quota): not waited out, never retried. */
  | "QUOTA_EXHAUSTED"
  | "CAPACITY_REJECTED"
  | "REQUEST_REJECTED"
  | "PERMANENT_FAILURE"
  | "AVAILABLE";

/**
 * What is known about whether the provider executed the failed request.
 * NOT_EXECUTED: proven not run (never sent, refused, or answered with a rejection status).
 * UNKNOWN: it may have been admitted and generated; nothing complete reached Nexus.
 * COMPLETED: the provider finished it (terminal evidence was received).
 */
export type ExecutionStatus = "NOT_EXECUTED" | "UNKNOWN" | "COMPLETED";

/** Retry metadata a provider advertised with a failure. All optional: plain OpenAI-compatible servers send none. */
export interface ProviderHints {
  retryAfterMs?: number;
  rateLimitResetMs?: number;
  remainingRequests?: number;
  remainingTokens?: number;
  /** Provider error code, e.g. `context_length_exceeded`, `gateway_restarting`, `pre_generation`. */
  errorCode?: string;
  errorType?: string;
}

/** One level of a transport error's cause chain (socket, TLS, or parser error beneath `fetch failed`). */
export interface TransportCause {
  name?: string;
  code?: string;
  errno?: number;
  syscall?: string;
  address?: string;
  port?: number;
  /** Bytes the socket had written/read when it failed; 0 written means the request never left this host. */
  bytesWritten?: number;
  bytesRead?: number;
  message?: string;
}

export interface InferenceFailure {
  kind: InferenceFailureKind;
  origin: InferenceFailureOrigin;
  message: string;
  httpStatus?: number;
  requestId?: string;
  /** Text received before the failure. Diagnostic only - never a complete answer. */
  partialTextChars?: number;
  /** Lower-level transport errors, outermost first. */
  transportCause?: TransportCause[];
  condition?: ProviderCondition;
  execution?: ExecutionStatus;
  hints?: ProviderHints;

/** One submission of an inference request that failed while the agent loop was recovering the provider. */
export interface RecoverySubmissionRecord {
  requestId: string;
  attempt: number;
  previousRequestId?: string;
  failedAt: string;
  kind: InferenceFailureKind;
  condition: ProviderCondition;
  execution: ExecutionStatus;
  httpStatus?: number;
  retryAfterMs?: number;
  message: string;

/**
 * Provider recovery for one inference step. WAITING/PROBING are live states (also checkpointed durably);
 * the rest are final. Created only when a submission fails.
 */
export interface ProviderRecoveryRecord {
  /** YIELDED: the operation scheduler took the step back (NOT_EXECUTED only) to reroute or park the work. */
  state: "WAITING" | "PROBING" | "RESUMED" | "EXHAUSTED" | "NOT_RECOVERABLE" | "CANCELLED" | "YIELDED";
  step: number;
  startedAt: string;
  updatedAt: string;
  nextAttemptAt?: string;
  resumedAt?: string;
  /** X-Request-ID of the submission that completed; it replaces the last entry of `submissions`. */
  resumedRequestId?: string;
  /** Latest provider condition observed by a submission or probe. */
  condition: ProviderCondition;
  reason?: string;
  submissions: RecoverySubmissionRecord[];
  probes: number;
  waitedMs: number;
  unknownReplays: number;
  endpoint?: string;
  everSucceeded?: boolean;
  policy: { deadlineMs: number; maxDelayMs: number; maxUnknownReplays: number };
}

export type VerificationStatus = "PASSED" | "FAILED" | "TIMED_OUT" | "NO_APPLICABLE_VERIFIER";

export interface VerificationEvidence {
  status: VerificationStatus;
  /** The verifier actually selected: configured override or one discovered from repository files. */
  command?: string;
  source?: "configured" | "discovered";
  exitSuccess?: boolean;
  hasExecutedTests?: boolean;
  isDeliverableBound?: boolean;
  /** True when the selected test command includes a filter and therefore cannot stand for the full suite. */
  filtered?: boolean;
  /**
   * A discovered verifier's pass is independent evidence of the change: tests that existed before it, unmodified,
   * failed before and pass after. False (with independenceDetail) when only the agent's own tests, or tests that also
   * passed before, check it — the turn is then REGRESSION_FREE, not VERIFIED.
   */
  independent?: boolean;
  independenceDetail?: string;
  /**
   * False when the workspace-resolved verifier definition could not be bound before the work (for example a
   * node_modules tree under `npm test`), so no pass can be independent evidence. The turn is then at most REGRESSION_FREE.
   */
  definitionBound?: false;
  /** Deadline the verifier was given, recorded when it timed out. */
  deadlineSecs?: number;
  outputSha256?: string;
  candidateId?: string;
  /** Type-check run beside the verifier. A scoped fact about the named configuration, never about the code in general. */
  typecheck?: TypecheckEvidence;
  at: string;
}

export interface TypecheckEvidence {
  /**
   * ENVIRONMENT: the check could not run or be attributed here (not a candidate failure). PREEXISTING: errors exist, but
   * none in a file the candidate modified; it is not a pass and does not block.
   */
  status: "PASSED" | "FAILED" | "TIMED_OUT" | "ENVIRONMENT" | "NOT_APPLICABLE" | "PREEXISTING" | "UNAVAILABLE";
  /** False when the result is recorded only (operator-configured verifier, or NEXUS_TYPECHECK mode "record"). */
  enforced?: boolean;
  tool?: string;
  toolVersion?: string;
  /** Hash of the resolved tool launcher. */
  toolSha256?: string;
  command?: string;
  configPath?: string;
  configSha256?: string;
  exitCode?: number | null;
  errorCount?: number;
  firstDiagnostics?: string[];
  /** Errors in the run that the pre-change baseline run did not have (present only when a baseline was captured). */
  introducedCount?: number;
  /** Errors the baseline run (before the change) already had. */
  baselineErrorCount?: number;
  /** Files counted as modified that no edit tool touched (changed through the shell), when any. */
  shellChangedFiles?: string[];
  /** What the result holds for: "under <configPath>", never universal. */
  scope?: string;
  /** Redacted, control characters made visible, capped, and fenced as untrusted compiler output. */
  excerpt?: string;
  candidateId?: string;
  at: string;
}

function planFromState(state: DurableOperationState): OperationGitPlan {
  const git = state.git!;
  const key = git.integrationBranch.split("/")[1]?.replace(/^op-/, "") ?? "op";
  return {
    key,
    repoRoot: git.repoRoot,
    baseRef: git.baseRef,
    baseCommit: git.baseCommit,
    integrationBranch: git.integrationBranch,
    integrationWorktree: git.integrationWorktree,
    baseDir: git.baseDir,
  };
}

export class OperationRunner {
  readonly registry: ResourceRegistry;
  readonly scheduler: ConvergenceScheduler;
  private readonly clock: RecoveryClock;
  private readonly revalidator: OperationRevalidator;
  private readonly git: OperationGit | undefined;
  /** One merge at a time: all units share the operation's integration worktree. */
  private integrationChain: Promise<void> = Promise.resolve();

  constructor(
    readonly state: DurableOperationState,
    private readonly opts: OperationRunnerOptions,
  ) {
    this.clock = opts.clock ?? realRecoveryClock;
    this.registry = new ResourceRegistry(state.resources, state.conditions, this.clock, (e) => this.onRegistryEvent(e));
    this.revalidator = new OperationRevalidator(opts.executor, this.registry, opts.onDiagnostic);
    this.scheduler = new ConvergenceScheduler(state, this.registry, () => this.clock.now(), opts.onEvent, opts.onDiagnostic);
    this.git = state.git?.isolate ? new OperationGit(planFromState(state), state.git) : undefined;
  }

  async run(signal?: AbortSignal): Promise<DurableOperationState> {
    const onAbort = () => {
      this.scheduler.cancel();
      this.save();
    };
    if (signal?.aborted) onAbort();
    else signal?.addEventListener("abort", onAbort, { once: true });
    try {
      return await this.runOperation(signal);
    } finally {
      signal?.removeEventListener("abort", onAbort);
    }
  }

  private async runOperation(signal?: AbortSignal): Promise<DurableOperationState> {
    if (this.state.status === "COMPLETE" || this.state.status === "CANCELLED") {
      this.git?.disposeAllUnits();
      return this.state;
    }
    if (this.git) {
      try {
        ensureIntegrationWorktree(planFromState(this.state), this.state.git!, {
          hasHistory:
            (this.state.integrations?.length ?? 0) > 0 ||
            Object.values(this.state.git!.units).some((entry) => entry.integratedCommit !== undefined),

# Nexus Code v1.2.1 plan

Status: PLAN, written 2026-11-15 against `main` plus the v1.2.0-rc.1 notes. Evidence and the full gap register are in [`GAP_ANALYSIS.md`](GAP_ANALYSIS.md); gap ids (GA-nn) refer to it. Owner decisions are recorded in section 6 (answered 2026-11-15) and nothing marked "decision" starts without one.

## 1. Purpose and theme

v1.2.0 made "done" mean something (independent verification, typed requirements, guarded verification files, convergence stopping, receipts with real dependencies) and said plainly that none of it is independent qualification. v1.2.1 is about **measuring it, shipping it to more people, containing it by default, and hardening what shipped**:

1. **Measure** the core claim (fewer false completions) on public benchmarks and on real projects.
2. **Reach**: platforms and integration points peers already have.
3. **Contain** by default, and close the record-only gaps.
4. **Harden** weak-model handling and context.
5. **Pay down** the process and maintainability debt that made v1.2.0 take a week of CI.

Non-goals: new verification features beyond the deferred SI-5/DV-3/DV-4 set, new providers, a hosted product, any claim of frontier-grade.

## 2. Rules for this release

- Every unit is test-first, one PR, with local Code / Security / Slop reviews on the exact head before merge (prompts: `memory/entire-agent-review-prompts.md`), required CI green at the exact head, and honest framing in notes: "ledger closed, qualification pending" until an external result exists.
- No new runtime dependency without an owner decision. No change to tags (immutable). Dependabot PRs roll in.
- A behaviour change that can break an existing user (containment default, concurrency validation, shell-write hard stop) is a decision (section 6), a release-notes line, and an opt-out.
- A unit that finds the plan wrong says so in its PR and updates this file.
- Live inference is the project's gateway only; any live measurement holds the `GATEWAY` claim and uses the key from the environment, never printed.

## 3. Release gates

v1.2.1 ships when:

| Gate | Condition |
|---|---|
| G-1 | `make test` green at the exact head; required CI green on the release commit; main CI green on the merge commit |
| G-2 | Every P0 unit merged; every P1 unit merged or carries a dated owner deferral |
| G-3 | Live-gateway tool-call matrix (G1.1-4) repeated on the release-candidate archive and recorded as evidence (also closes GA-03 for v1.2.0 if still open) |
| G-4 | A first external-style measurement exists and is published in the notes with its limits (MQ-2): at minimum a pinned Terminal-Bench subset run through the Harbor adapter, with the false-completion rate reported beside the pass rate. If no run is possible in the window, the notes say "no external measurement" and the release is still allowed; the framing never changes |
| G-5 | No test in the suite can leak a bridge, agent, gateway, child process or timer past its file (PC-2 guard green) |
| G-6 | Docs: README, CHANGELOG, manual and examples current (DH-1…DH-3) |

"Externally qualified" is defined in section 7 so the word has one meaning.

## Process lessons from v1.2.1

- A release workflow runs tests that pull-request CI skips (host-conditional ones); run those under a flooded environment before tagging.
- A background agent's reported test subset is not the suite: two failures in the VC-9 PR were found only by CI.
- An agent's own mutation report is not evidence until re-run; one PR had a surviving mutation, another reported a mutation as caught when it was not.
- CI colours its output and runs on Node 22 and 24 with different timing: agent PRs need local runs with `FORCE_COLOR=1 CI=true`, and tables kept in sync by a test (such as the global option table in `eval_cli.ts`) need the new flag added in the same change. Two real failures in the `--fork-session` PR and one in the VC-9 PR were found only by CI.
- A timing-sensitive PTY test (`the whole live TUI through a pseudo-terminal`) failed once on Node 22 in the VC-7 PR and passed on rerun; it is a known-flaky class (see `flake-report`), recorded here rather than hidden.
- A background agent can stall behind its own watcher loops for hours; give agents a foreground-only rule and check their worktree for changes when a status request goes unanswered.
# Nexus Code v1.3 plan: the platform track

Status: PLAN, written 2026-11-15 against `main` plus the v1.2.0-rc.1 notes, at the owner's request ("draft the v1.3 platform track as recommended"). It follows v1.2.1 and v1.2.2 ([`docs/v1.2.1/PLAN.md`](../v1.2.1/PLAN.md), decision D12). Nothing here is a claim that Nexus Code is frontier-grade, and no unit starts without the decisions in section 7.

## 1. Purpose and theme

Frontier clients are platforms: a CLI plus a desktop app, IDE integration, background and scheduled agents, an SDK or managed API, installable plugin bundles, and enterprise policy (web sources of 2026-11-15, mostly third-party; see [`docs/v1.2.1/GAP_ANALYSIS.md`](../v1.2.1/GAP_ANALYSIS.md) §2). Nexus is a single-binary Linux CLI and TUI. It cannot match breadth or first-party model fit, and a worse copy of three funded platforms is not a goal.

The v1.3 theme: **let other programs drive Nexus and let teams govern it, without weakening the gate.** Every new surface (an IDE over ACP, a scheduler, a hook, a plugin, an SDK caller, a managed policy) goes through the same approval and verification gates as the terminal does. The differentiator to build on is the one nobody else ships by default: a completion you can audit (independent verification, receipts, evidence). Two consequences shape the plan:

1. **Nexus as the verification layer for other harnesses.** `nexus verify` and an MCP/ACP `verify` tool let a Codex, Claude Code or Aider session ask Nexus to independently check its work. This costs little (the machinery exists) and is positioned where the platforms are weakest.
2. **Governance as a product.** Managed policy with fixed precedence, a hash-chained and optionally signed audit export, and hooks that can only tighten.

Non-goals: a marketplace, a desktop or mobile app, a Nexus-specific VS Code extension (ACP clients already exist), hosted or multi-tenant operation (dropped 2026-11-15, decision D8), plugin auto-update, any new runtime dependency without a decision.

## 2. Evidence and its limits

- **Nexus today** (read-only inventory, 2026-11-15; "present" means present in source or docs, nothing was run): sidecar/TUI protocol is NDJSON over the sidecar's stdio with `PROTOCOL_VERSION = 1`, an event `v`, a one-way `hello`, typed unions in `cli/src/protocol.ts:53-204` hand-mirrored in `core/src/bin/nexus_tui/protocol.rs`, **no schema file, no socket**; `nexus run --json` returns `TaskExecutionResult` (`cli/src/core/app.ts:44`) with no schema or version, exit codes defined only in code (0 verified, 2 completed-unverified, 130 interrupted, 1 otherwise); `ApplicationCore` is an accidental re-export (`cli/src/index.ts:1240`) and `cli/package.json` has `main` and `bin` but no `exports` or `types`; operations are durable and resumable (per-operation lock, 12 h wait survives restart, `maxConcurrentUnits` capped at 64 and clamped to 1 without `git.isolate`) but **foreground-only**, with no scheduler, cron, trigger or daemon in the code; plugins are plain JS modules with no manifest, checksum or install command, workspace plugins load after `nexus trust` with full process authority, hooks cover pre/post tool only; policy is the workspace-local `.nexus-security.json`, **fails open to defaults on a parse error**, with no system or admin layer; session export is `nexus-session-export/2` reachable only through `/export`; the flight log is append-only by convention (no hash chain found) and the CERI evidence store hashes files but has no signature or verify command; local OTLP-style traces are written on every session with no opt-in gate and no network exporter found; a goal (objective ledger) persists across sessions via `--resume`, but nothing re-launches a task on its own.
- **Peers, read from source** (shallow clones of 2026-11-13/14; Codex at commit 336b19a; untrusted code, nothing run): ACP servers in goose (`crates/goose/src/acp`), Cline (`apps/cli/src/acp/acpAgent.ts`), Gemini CLI (`packages/cli/src/acp`) and opencode (`packages/cli/src/acp/agent.ts`), the Codex `app-server` (JSON-RPC 2.0 over stdio, websocket or UDS; schema generated from Rust types and checked in); schedulers in goose (`scheduler/full.rs`), Cline (`*.cron.md` and event specs) and opencode (a `ScheduleTable` with `in`/`at`/`every`/`cron` and an optional deterministic wake `check`); hooks in Gemini CLI (`docs/hooks/reference.md`), goose (`hooks/mod.rs`), Cline and Codex; extension manifests in Gemini CLI (`gemini-extension.json`), goose (Open Plugins and Gemini formats) and opencode; policy tiers in Gemini CLI (`core/src/policy/config.ts:67-71`), opencode (`managed-policy.ts`) and Codex (`requirements.toml`); goal state in opencode (`schema/src/goal.ts`) and Codex (`thread/goal/*`).

- **Research notes** (2026-11-15): the Anthropic 2026 agentic coding trends report (read in full; a vendor document with no methodology, customer-reported figures) and OpenHands (documentation, not source) support three priorities here: VR-1 and VR-2 (the report's own evidence is that people delegate what is cheaply checkable, so verifiability is the delegation boundary), PA-1 (it names a view of concurrent agent sessions) and AC-1 (above). They are framing, not evidence about Nexus.
- **Not covered:** Claude Code and agy were not read (web sources only); parts of Cline's daemon, Codex's hook handler types and plugin manifest, and goose's managed policy were sampled, not read in full; peer behaviour under load was not measured.

## 3. Principles

1. **Protocol first.** Nothing else in this plan is safe to build until the client protocol is published, schema'd, versioned and conformance-tested.
2. **One gate.** A new surface can request an approval but can never answer one on behalf of Nexus's own gates (SI-2, CS-* rules, verification). A client that answers "allow" to a denied action must have no effect; this is tested.
3. **Tighten only.** Hooks and managed policy may deny, require a human, or rewrite arguments toward safer values. They never grant.
4. **Unattended means stricter.** Scheduled and detached runs never get allow-always, run in a fresh worktree, and record that they were unattended in every receipt.
5. **Explicit trust.** Project-defined hooks, plugins and policy run only after a trust decision keyed by a content hash; a changed file asks again.
6. **Schemas come from types.** Generate JSON Schema from the TypeScript types and check it in with a parity test, so the Rust mirror cannot drift (reference: Codex `app-server-protocol` schema export, goose `acp-schema.json`).
7. **No new runtime dependency** without a decision. ACP is plain JSON-RPC; hash chains and ed25519 signing use `node:crypto`.
8. **Experimental is a flag.** New methods sit behind `experimental` at `initialize` (reference: Codex `experimentalApi`) until a conformance suite has run against two real clients.

# Nexus Code v1.2.1 plan

Status: PLAN, written 2026-11-15 against `main` plus the v1.2.0-rc.1 notes. Evidence and the full gap register are in [`GAP_ANALYSIS.md`](GAP_ANALYSIS.md); gap ids (GA-nn) refer to it. Owner decisions are recorded in section 6 (answered 2026-11-15) and nothing marked "decision" starts without one.

## 1. Purpose and theme

v1.2.0 made "done" mean something (independent verification, typed requirements, guarded verification files, convergence stopping, receipts with real dependencies) and said plainly that none of it is independent qualification. v1.2.1 is about **measuring it, shipping it to more people, containing it by default, and hardening what shipped**:

1. **Measure** the core claim (fewer false completions) on public benchmarks and on real projects.
2. **Reach**: platforms and integration points peers already have.
3. **Contain** by default, and close the record-only gaps.
4. **Harden** weak-model handling and context.
5. **Pay down** the process and maintainability debt that made v1.2.0 take a week of CI.

Non-goals: new verification features beyond the deferred SI-5/DV-3/DV-4 set, new providers, a hosted product, any claim of frontier-grade.

## 2. Rules for this release

- Every unit is test-first, one PR, with local Code / Security / Slop reviews on the exact head before merge (prompts: `memory/entire-agent-review-prompts.md`), required CI green at the exact head, and honest framing in notes: "ledger closed, qualification pending" until an external result exists.
- No new runtime dependency without an owner decision. No change to tags (immutable). Dependabot PRs roll in.
- A behaviour change that can break an existing user (containment default, concurrency validation, shell-write hard stop) is a decision (section 6), a release-notes line, and an opt-out.
- A unit that finds the plan wrong says so in its PR and updates this file.
- Live inference is the project's gateway only; any live measurement holds the `GATEWAY` claim and uses the key from the environment, never printed.

## 3. Release gates

v1.2.1 ships when:

| Gate | Condition |
|---|---|
| G-1 | `make test` green at the exact head; required CI green on the release commit; main CI green on the merge commit |
| G-2 | Every P0 unit merged; every P1 unit merged or carries a dated owner deferral |
| G-3 | Live-gateway tool-call matrix (G1.1-4) repeated on the release-candidate archive and recorded as evidence (also closes GA-03 for v1.2.0 if still open) |
| G-4 | A first external-style measurement exists and is published in the notes with its limits (MQ-2): at minimum a pinned Terminal-Bench subset run through the Harbor adapter, with the false-completion rate reported beside the pass rate. If no run is possible in the window, the notes say "no external measurement" and the release is still allowed; the framing never changes |
| G-5 | No test in the suite can leak a bridge, agent, gateway, child process or timer past its file (PC-2 guard green) |
| G-6 | Docs: README, CHANGELOG, manual and examples current (DH-1…DH-3) |

"Externally qualified" is defined in section 7 so the word has one meaning.

## 4. Workstreams and units

Size: S = one PR; M = two to four PRs; L = a program. P0 = must-have, P1 = should-have, P2 = stretch (may roll to v1.2.2).
