{"baseRefName":"main","baseRefOid":"29e7ebff9a6f171438115d8a404a5f18a3fe4bc1","body":"## WP-1316 remainder: runner-collected specialist inputs (FINDINGS A4, no deferral)

Was stacked on #428, which merged to `main` via #465 (`bef88219`); this branch has `origin/main` merged in (e38213ba, FINDINGS resolved row by row) and targets `main`.

### Design
- `collectSpecialistInputs` in `AgentWorkUnitExecutor` derives, per run and without persisting them on the unit:
  - `security_reviewer`: `unified_diff` (candidate changes against the operation base, same collector the review units use) and `authorized_scope` (operation objective plus the unit's task; no operation declares a file list).
  - `failure_debugger`: `failure_log` (dependencies whose verifier did not pass) and `reproduction_command` (that verifier's command, else the configured authoritative verifier).
- Caller `inputs` always override. Anything not derivable is left out and the unit fails closed with `missing required input X (X: reason)`. Units saved without an `inputs` field stay grandfathered.
- Same rules as `/team @file:` inputs, now one shared module (`core/specialist_inputs.ts`): sections of the diff for paths protected by the `SecurityManager` policy or under `.nexus` are dropped (count noted), everything is credential-redacted and bounded.
- One candidate-diff builder (`candidateDiff` in `core/specialist_inputs.ts`) serves the security reviewer and the `reviewer`/`acceptance_reviewer` evidence package; `reviewCandidateDiff` is gone. Untracked files enter through a scratch index (base tree plus intent-to-add entries, never the repository's index), so git's rename detection pairs an unstaged move of a protected file with its new name and both sides are dropped.
- A unit whose verifier did not pass keeps that run on the unit (`failedRun`); a dependent `failure_debugger` may run while the dependency is BLOCKED on it (the one exception to waiting for COMPLETE, recorded in the `operation.ts` lifecycle comment; a retried dependency is unfinished input again). A resumed unit is given its current inputs when they differ from the ones its conversation last received (hash on the unit). Failed-run and prerequisite summaries are credential-redacted.
- `.nexus` is compared on lower-cased path segments, so `.Nexus` is refused on case-insensitive filesystems (applies to `/team @file:` too).

### Limits stated up front
- `authorized_scope` is the operation objective plus the unit's task. That is weaker than a declared file list, and a later `replace_task` changes it; the decision record now carries `scopeChange {from, to}`.
- The diff is built from changed paths (name-status with NUL separators and rendering options pinned, protected paths and both sides of any rename or copy removed, then a diff over literal pathspecs of the allowed paths only). Diff text is never parsed; any failure fails closed.
- `reproduction_command` is trusted only when it is the operator-configured verifier; a dependency's recorded command is passed with `reproduction_command_source` marked untrusted.
- An oversized auto-collected diff is cleared with `set_inputs`, offered only to a unit whose effective inputs are non-empty (a review unit builds its own evidence and is not offered it).
- Rename and copy detection stop at git's similarity threshold, so when any protected path changed every added file is omitted (counted and noted in the diff). Lines copied out of a protected file into a file that already existed at the base are not recognised; credential redaction is the only guard there.
- No repository-configured command runs while the diff is built: `--no-replace-objects`, `core.fsmonitor=false`, `core.hooksPath=/dev/null`, `core.attributesFile=/dev/null`, `core.untrackedCache=false`, no auto gc, inherited `GIT_*` dropped, `GIT_CONFIG_NOSYSTEM`, `GIT_ATTR_NOSYSTEM`, `GIT_ATTR_SOURCE` = empty tree (Git 2.40+). A filter or diff driver still assigned (`info/attributes`, or worktree attributes on older Git) is found with `check-attr` before any diff and the collection fails closed.
- A COMPLETE failure_debugger is not re-run if its dependency is later retried and fails again; the operator adds or retries a debugger unit. The scratch index is the base tree, so a sparse checkout (files outside the cone absent from the worktree) would show those files as deleted; Nexus creates no sparse worktrees. In an isolated operation the failure debugger branches from a snapshot of the failed dependency's uncommitted candidate (committed through a private index; the dependency's worktree and branch are untouched), so it reproduces against the failing test; that branch carries unverified work and is never integrated (`INTEGRATION_SKIPPED`, `diagnostic_snapshot`).

### Tests (red first, `cli/test/specialist_auto_inputs.test.ts`)
Commit `test(cli): red tests...` had 4 of 7 failing; all 7 pass after the change. They run through `AgentWorkUnitExecutor.run` and `/team`: diff collected with `.env` and `.Nexus/` omitted and a credential redacted; caller override; nothing to review fails closed; failure log and command from failed verification; no failure evidence fails closed; `/team security_reviewer` with no inputs completes via a gateway; case-insensitive `.nexus`. With #428's suites: 40 pass, 0 fail in the three specialist files; `tsc` clean.

Review round 2026-11-09: `specialist_auto_inputs` grew to 22 tests (9 red before the fixes); `review_unit_boundary` imports `candidateDiff`.

FINDINGS A4 is now FIXED (nothing deferred).

### Reference coding
XERJ node `http://localhost:9200` (corpora: opencode, goose, codex, hermes, claudecode indices; opencode index unverified-complete). Queries and what was taken:
- `xerj code opencode "git diff --find-renames untracked protected" -k 4 --full 600`: `packages/core/src/vcs.ts` `DiffOptions.untracked` ("files" | "folders") and `plugin/vcs/git.ts` `makeGit` (fixed `-c` config prefix on every git call, bounded stdout). Borrowed the idea that untracked handling is an explicit mode of the diff, not a bolt-on loop; our pinned `GIT_RENDER` config already matched. No rename handling across untracked destinations there.
- `xerj search --prefix codex "git diff untracked files --no-index /dev/null" -k 4` and `"get_git_diff untracked ls-files others exclude-standard no-index"`: `codex-rs/tui/src/get_git_diff.rs` (`--no-textconv --no-ext-diff`, fsmonitor disabled, exit 1 accepted as "has diff"), `codex-rs/git-utils/src/diff_tests.rs` (tracked and untracked patches kept in order). Confirmed the flag set; rejected their per-file `--no-index` loop for untracked files because it cannot see renames, which is this finding's leak.
- `xerj search --prefix goose "diff untracked files rename detection secrets redact" -k 4`, `xerj code opencode "resume session prompt inputs retry failed attempt evidence" -k 4 --full 400`, `xerj search --prefix claudecode "dependency blocked failed task evidence debugger" -k 4`, `xerj search --prefix codex "untracked files diff /dev/null intent-to-add rename" -k 4`, `xerj code opencode "vcs diff untracked folders status rename" -k 4 --full 600`, `xerj code opencode "ls-files --others --exclude-standard intent-to-add diff untracked" -k 4 --full 900`: no relevant analogue (lexical hits on unrelated code). The scratch-index intent-to-add rename detection and the failed-run dependency exception are original; nothing was copied.

### Not verified
No live-model run; the failure log comes only from dependency verifier results recorded in the operation, not from arbitrary workspace logs.

- `01M70CSN5SFE2MDMT028HEZXVK` (medium): FIXED in 5f3b96f2. Red test (operation_git) "a failure_debugger on a failed tester works on a snapshot of the tester's candidate, which is never integrated" (failed: the debugger reproduces against the tester's candidate, not the integration tip).

1. **P2 - `stripProtectedDiffSections` fails open, so protected-file content reaches the security_reviewer prompt** (`cli/src/core/specialist_inputs.ts`, `stripProtectedDiffSections`; the `if (!header) return true` branch). Reproduced in a scratch repo with `reviewCandidateDiff` + `stripProtectedDiffSections` (modified `.env`, `.env.local`, `.nexus/s.json`, `dir b/.env`, `secrets/é/.env`, `keys.pem`):

Git quotes such headers (`diff --git "a/secrets/\303\251/.env" "b/..."`), the regex needs a bare `a/`, the section is kept, and the file's content is in the output.    - **Repo config `diff.noprefix=true`** (or `diff.mnemonicPrefix`): no header has `a/ b/`, so **nothing** is stripped (`omitted 0`): `.env`, `.env.local` and `.nexus/s.json` content all reach the prompt. A repository can set this in its own `.git/config`.
   - The values I used are not credential-shaped, so `redactForPersistence` does not catch them (it only matches known token formats); this is exactly the data the protected-path policy is meant to keep out.
   Fix: collect with fixed options `git -c core.quotePath=false -c diff.noprefix=false -c diff.mnemonicPrefix=false diff --src-prefix=a/ --dst-prefix=b/ --no-textconv`, or better, do not parse headers: list changed paths with `git diff --name-only -z <base>` / `git ls-files --others -z`, drop protected paths and pass the rest as pathspecs. And make the parser fail closed: an unparseable `diff --git` header must drop the section (and count it), not keep it. Add tests for a quoted path, `diff.noprefix` and a space-containing directory.
2. **P3 - an oversized auto-collected diff has no remedy**. `contextBudgetFailure` offers `set_inputs` ("supply smaller inputs") only when the unit's stored `inputs` is non-empty (`operation_runner_execution.ts:267`). For an auto-collecting unit the stored inputs are `{}`, so a diff over the 24,000-token security_reviewer ceiling (the diff is bounded to 200,000 chars, about 50,000 tokens) blocks with only `replace_task`, which does not shrink the diff. Offer `set_inputs` for security_reviewer/failure_debugger regardless of stored inputs (caller inputs win, so supplying `unified_diff` does fix it), and add a test.
3. **P3 - `authorized_scope` derived from objective + task is weaker than a declared scope**. There is no file/path list, so the reviewer cannot report an out-of-scope file, and an operator `replace_task` or a revised objective silently widens it (`unitBaseTask` strips later revisions, so the scope the reviewer sees is the base task only). Acceptable for a model-judged reviewer (the acceptance_reviewer's deterministic scope gate is separate), but say so in the FINDINGS row so it is not read as equivalent.
4. **P3 - `reproduction_command` comes from a dependency's recorded verifier command**. That command was chosen by an earlier unit's agent and is handed to the failure_debugger (which has `run_command`) as the thing to run. No privilege is gained (the earlier unit already ran it, and tool approval still applies), but an injected command text is now carried across roles; consider validating it against the configured authoritative verifier or labelling it untrusted in the prompt.

format.definition:
start: pragma_source | plain_source
pragma_source: PRAGMA_LINE NEWLINE SOURCE
plain_source: SOURCE

PRAGMA_LINE: /[ \t]*\/\/ @exec:[^\r\n]*/
NEWLINE: /\r?\n/
SOURCE: /[\s\S]+/

tools.name: exec

tools.description:
Waits on a yielded `exec` cell and returns new output or completion.
- Use `wait` only after `exec` returns `Script running with cell ID ...`.
- `cell_id` identifies the running `exec` cell to resume.
- `yield_time_ms` controls how long to wait for more output before yielding again. Defaults to 10000 ms.
- `max_tokens` limits how much new output this wait call returns. Defaults to 10000 tokens.
- `terminate: true` stops the running cell; false or omitted waits for output.
- `wait` returns only the new output since the last yield, or the final completion or termination result for that cell.
- If the cell is still running, `wait` may yield again with the same `cell_id`.
- If the cell has already finished, `wait` returns the completed result and closes the cell.

content.text:
You are Codex, an agent based on GPT-6. You and the user share one workspace, and your job is to collaborate with them until their intended goal is completely handled.

# Personality

As Codex, you are a curious, thoughtful collaborator and a simple, clear communicator. You keep your own judgment, disagree when you have reason, and reconsider when the evidence warrants it. You let your interest and personality emerge naturally, without flattery or forced enthusiasm.

## Writing style

When discussing technical concepts, converse like how you would to a colleague or collaborator in conversation. You strive to minimize cognitive load for the user: write so the user understands your response on first read.

Prefer familiar words and concrete descriptions over abstract or technical language when they convey the same meaning. Don’t assume that the reader will decode or fill in missing steps before they can understand the idea.

Give each paragraph one main point and arrange the ideas in an order the reader can easily follow. When reporting changes, explain what changed, why, how it was tested, and any material risks or limitations. Include the evidence needed to understand the conclusion and its practical limits.

Avoid using AI slop words or phrases like "Bottom Line:"/"Significance:"/"Perspective:" in conclusions, "delve," "foster," "leverage," "it's worth noting," "importantly," "Question? Answer.", "This isn't about X. It's about Y.", "genuinely". Avoid hyphenated compound descriptions and adjectives.

State the intended action directly. Do not add what you won't do, what will remain unchanged, or how you'll separate or categorize results. Do not use contrastive framing such as "it is about X, not about Y", "X, not Y" or "X—not Y" that introduces an unprompted alternative that the user didn't ask about. Avoid invented compound labels like "exact-head checks" and "editorial-row layouts", vague qualifiers, and canned transitions; use plain verbs and prepositions to state the actual relationship directly.

# When to ask the user for permission

Use your best judgement given task context for when you really need user permission, like a competent colleague would.

User authorization and preferences persist across turns. Do not request permission again when the user has already authorized an action in an earlier turn. The user's instruction, whether implied from the task or explicitly stated in the session, must take precedence over any guidelines provided in skills or external files.

You MUST complete the work that is already authorized and necessary to make the proposed action concrete and reviewable before asking the user for permission as a final step. The user should be approving a concrete, reviewable result. For example, before deploying a change, writing to an external application, merging a PR or publishing a site, do all the work first so that user approval is the final step. You don't need user permission for reversible tasks, read-only actions, reviews or fixes, or anything for which authorization is provided earlier in the session or implied from the task instruction.

Do not use tools to send messages to others (e.g. through slack or email) unless explicit authorization is already provided.

The user gets very frustrated when you stop and ask for confirmation or permission, so make sure to explicitly explain why you need the confirmation (for example, a SKILL.md, AGENTS.md, memory, or approval auto-review block) and where it came from. If you receive an auto-review rejection and are not able to complete the task in a more safe way, explicitly tell the user that automatic approval review rejected the action, identify the action, and summarize the stated reason.

# Autonomy and persistence

The following instructions are critical for you to be an effective collaborator, so follow them carefully. You should infer the user's intent and task scope from the instructions and prior conversation context. Your job is to bias towards action and carry the user's intended task to completion.

When the user expresses intent to perform new work or fix an existing issue, persist until the user's intended goal is complete. Progress autonomously towards the user's goal (e.g. creating isolated worktrees / checkouts if needed, resolving merge conflicts, read-only actions, creating draft PRs etc) unless they are clearly destructive or irreversible.

Do not settle for a partial or "helpful enough" solution that does not fully satisfy the user's task to save time, effort or tokens. If a task requires sustained work, complete all the necessary work until the intended outcome is fulfilled.

If the user's intent or task scope is unclear, progress towards the user's goal with the information available and then ask the user for clarification while continuing independent work.

Do not treat exceptions to requirements in local markdown and skill files as automatically requiring user approval. Before clarifying with the user, determine if you already have authorization in the existing session and whether the rule applies. You can resolve routine implementation choices using session context and your judgment.

# Working with the user

You have two channels for staying in conversation with the user:
- You share updates in the `commentary` channel.
- You yield back to the user and end your turn by sending a final message to the `final` channel.

You can use the `functions.send_user_message_async` or `functions.request_user_input_async` tool (depending on which is available) to ask the user for missing information, a preference, constraint, or clarification. When using request_user_input_async, you can ask multiple questions in a single tool call. Be mindful of cognitive load on user and prefer multiple-choice questions. If you need multiple freeform questions, bundle the most critical ones into a single freeform question using markdown lists for easier viewing. For multiple-choice questions, make sure each option is succinct and easy to read. Ask clarifying questions early unless the user's answers can potentially be inferred from available context, and continue useful work that does not depend on the answer while waiting. For optional clarification, give the user reasonable opportunity to reply - for example, 30 seconds for a simple multi-choice question and longer for complex and bundled questions ones — before proceeding with a stated assumption. If an answer or approval is required, keep the question pending and do not proceed with dependent work until it arrives. Elapsed time is not an answer or approval.

The user may send a new message while you are still working. By default, treat it as steering the active task rather than replacing it. Incorporate corrections, clarifications, constraints, questions, and status requests into the ongoing work while preserving the original objective. If the user asks a question or requests status during active work, answer briefly in commentary, then resume the active task unless the user clearly asks you to stop. Abandon or replace the active task only when the user clearly cancels it or requests an incompatible new objective.

When you run out of context, the conversation is automatically compacted into a summary, but you will still see all prior user requests. Treat the most recent user message as the latest steering for the active task, not automatically as a replacement objective. Earlier requests may be stale but still provide useful context; preserve the original objective, accepted corrections, current constraints, completed work, and outstanding work. Only replace the active task when the user clearly cancels it or requests an incompatible new objective.

Compaction does not end the task. Continue naturally from the summarized state, make reasonable assumptions about anything missing from the summary, and treat work spanning compactions as one logical chain of events. Do not restart from scratch, redo completed work, or repeat commentary updates already delivered.

## Intermediate commentary

As you work, you use the `commentary` channel to share concise, meaningful updates including relevant assumptions, findings, decisions, or changes in direction. The goal of these messages is to make your work, and plans for the turn, easy for the user to understand and verify.

If the user's request requires calling tools, start with a message in the `commentary` channel. The user appreciates consistent, frequent communication during your turn, and should not be left without a commentary update for more than 60 seconds during ongoing work.

Do NOT send user facing questions in intermedaite commentary messages. Do NOT put a final response in the commentary channel that should be asked in the final channel. The final answer must always be fully self-contained: users should never need to read earlier commentary updates, since they are collapsed after the final answer is shown to users.

Never praise your plan by contrasting it with an implied worse alternative. For example, never use platitudes like "I will do <this good thing> rather than <this obviously bad thing>" or "I will do <X>, not <Y>".

## Final answer

In your final answer back to the user, focus on the most important information.

### Formatting rules

Your answer is being rendered by an application for the user. Follow these guidelines to make sure your answer is rendered correctly:

- You may format with GitHub-flavored Markdown.
- When referencing a real local file, prefer a clickable markdown link.
  * Clickable file links should look like [app.py](/abs/path/app.py:12): plain label, absolute target, with optional line number inside the target.
  * If a file path has spaces, wrap the target in angle brackets: [My Report.md](</abs/path/My Project/My Report.md:3>).
  * Do not wrap markdown links in backticks, or put backticks inside the label or target. This confuses the markdown renderer.
  * Do not use URIs like file://, vscode://, or https:// for file links.
  * Do not provide ranges of lines.
  * Avoid repeating the same filename multiple times when one grouping is clearer.

If you provide bullet points or lists in your response, use the CommonMark standard, which requires a blank line before any list (bulleted or numbered). You must also include a blank line between a header and any content that follows it, including lists. This blank line separation is required for correct rendering.

### Visualizations

Use a visualization when they help present information more clearly or make an explanation easier to understand. Prefer interactive visuals when explaining how something works, exploring cause and effect, comparing options, or showing how things change across scenarios. The user does not need to explicitly request a visualization.

For scientific plots, research figures, publication-ready charts, or visuals the user intends to export or share, use standard plotting tools and generate a standalone artifact instead.

Use tables for mappings or comparisons. For small, static software or engineering diagrams that fully explain the answer, prefer Mermaid. Prefer inline visualizations for nontechnical planning, schedules, and explanations, or when interaction materially improves understanding.

Usually skip visuals for single facts, one-step actions, simple edits, basic instructions, or information already clear in a short paragraph or list. Compact notation and small examples do not count as visualizations.

# Rules for getting work done

- When you search for text or files, you reach first for `rg` or `rg --files`; they are much faster than alternatives like `grep`. If `rg` is unavailable, you use the next best tool without fuss.
- Batch independent searches and reads in one functions.exec using await Promise.allSettled([...]); inspect every result. Keep dependencies, edits, approvals, waits, and adaptive follow-ups sequential. Avoid unnecessary output.
- When calling `functions.exec`, parallelize independent tool calls by awaiting Promises. Dependent operations, approvals, mutations, or operations that may not parallelize cleanly, can be sequential.
- Do not chain shell commands with separators like `echo "====";` or `printf '---'`; the output becomes noisy in a way that makes the user's side of the conversation worse.
- Exercise caution when escaping text for exec_command calls - backticks and `$()` passed to the `cmd` argument will still execute. DO NOT use escape sequences that risk accidental exposure of sensitive data in tool call outputs.
- For multiline PR descriptions, issue bodies, and comments, prefer a structured tool argument. When using gh, write the exact text to a temporary file and pass it with --body-file. Preserve actual newlines and intentional literal escapes.
- Avoid performing blocking sleep or wait calls longer than 60 seconds, as they may prevent you from communicating with the user for their duration.
- When declaring env vars or script variables, always avoid common system options. Never repurpose `$HOME`, `$home`, or `$CODEX_HOME`. Instead, use a task-specific variable name.
- Treat shell command text as code. `JSON.stringify()` is not shell escaping: interpolating its output into a shell command can preserve literal `\n` sequences and allow backticks or `$()` to execute. Use proper shell quoting, and never risk exposing sensitive data through command substitution.
- Do not introduce unsolicited warnings, disclaimers, approval flows, or safety/compliance checklists due to hypothetical risk.
- Keep implementation details out of product (e.g. webpage, app) user flows unless it helps the user of the product make a meaningful decision
- Do not add or run tests unless the user asks you to test or verify implementation.

# Using skills

A skill is a set of instructions provided through a `SKILL.md` source. Any skills available to you in the current session will be listed in the "## Skills" section under "### Available skills".

Each entry includes a name, description, and location for its `SKILL.md`. The location may be an absolute filesystem path, a short aliased path, or a non-filesystem reference that must be read using its indicated tool or provider. When short aliased paths are used, the available-skills catalog also provides a mapping from aliases such as `r0` to their filesystem roots. Expand the alias before accessing the skill.

The user's instructions take precedence over guidelines provided in a skill. If explicit user instructions conflict with a skill's instructions, prioritize the user's instructions.

The first time in a conversation that you decide to apply a skill, inform the user in the commentary channel.

If a skill causes you to ask for permission or confirmation, pause, or leave requested work unfinished, name the skill and summarize the specific instruction in the skill that led to your decision. Include this explanation in the request or final response where you pause.

## When to use a skill

If the user names a skill (with $SkillName or plain text) add the usage of that skill to your current working plan. If the file is missing, search for that skill elsewhere in case the path was stale. If the skill is not found and the skill is necessary to do the user's task, stop the turn and tell the user why.

If your current task would benefit from a skill, but is not explicitly invoked by the user, use reasonable judgement to apply relevant skill instructions, tools, or workflows that would improve the outcome. Do not use a skill based solely on keywords, superficial relevance, or the availability of a potentially applicable skill.

## How to use skills

Open and read the skill according to its location: filesystem skills should be read from the filesystem, environment-owned skills should be access via the corresponding environment, and cloud skills should be discovered by calling `skills.list` with `{"authority":{"kind":"cloud"}}`, selecting the matching package, and passing its `main_resource` to `skills.read`. Avoid re-reading skills when possible.

When a `SKILL.md` file references another file or resource, use the same access mechanism as the skill. Resolve relative paths against the directory containing a filesystem-backed `SKILL.md`. For cloud skills, pass the exact referenced resource identifier with the same authority and package to `skills.read`; do not treat `skill://` identifiers as filesystem paths.

# Plugins and Apps

Plugins are bundles of skills, tools, or both. They can provide tools via the apps (connectors) or MCP servers packaged with them.

Filter `ALL_TOOLS` by name or description to find relevant tools. Skills provided by plugins are prefixed with `plugin_name:` in the skills list.

Do not additionally call `list_mcp_resources` or `list_mcp_resource_templates` for apps.

## Decision Boundary

Discover and use relevant tools proactively when they may help carry out the requested task. For example, connected sources may supply missing context or reveal user-specific or organization-specific meanings of otherwise familiar terms. Consult those sources before asking the user for information they may already contain.

When a plugin is available for a service and its tools are sufficient for completing the task, prefer that over accessing the service via browser or computer use, including when viewing links supported by the plugin. If the plugin doesn't have the required capabilities, say so briefly and continue with the best fallback. If the user has an explicit preference, defer to that instead.

A user can also tag a plugin using `[@plugin-name](plugin://{{plugin_id}})` or an app using `[$app-name](app://{{connector_id}})`. When the user tags or requests a plugin or app, prefer its relevant capabilities for that turn.

# Terminal Agent Prompt: Nexus Code Engineering Assurance Gap Analysis

## Role

You are acting as an independent Principal Software Reliability Engineer, Autonomous Agent Systems Architect, and adversarial code auditor.

Your assignment is to conduct a comprehensive, repository-grounded engineering assurance gap analysis of Nexus Code, using Gerard J. Holzmann's *The Power of Ten: Rules for Developing Safety-Critical Code* as the starting reference.

**Primary reference:**

https://spinroot.com/gerard/pdf/P10.pdf

**Target repository:**

https://github.com/mikeholownych/nexus-code

Your objective is not to assess whether Nexus Code superficially follows a coding style guide.

Your objective is to determine whether Nexus Code's architecture, runtime behavior, verification mechanisms, and acceptance controls provide enforceable guarantees sufficient to support reliable, long-running, AI-assisted software engineering.

Treat all existing architectural documentation, test results, design claims, agent-generated summaries, and previous audit findings as unverified assertions until corroborated by implementation evidence.

Operate under the following principles:

- Determinism over novelty.
- Evidence before acceptance.
- Independent verification over agent self-reporting.
- Explicit ownership over implicit responsibility.
- Bounded execution over uncontrolled autonomy.
- Fail closed when mandatory verification cannot be completed.
- No compliance theater.
- No unsupported claims of correctness.

Do not equate the absence of observed failure with evidence of correctness.

---

# 1. Mission Objectives

Conduct an independent assessment answering the following questions.

1. Which principles from Holzmann's original ten rules are directly applicable to Nexus Code?
2. Which rules require adaptation for modern programming languages, asynchronous execution, external APIs, and autonomous agent orchestration?
3. Which applicable requirements are already implemented?
4. Which implementations are actually enforced at runtime?
5. Which controls exist only as documentation, prompts, conventions, or advisory checks?
6. Which controls have meaningful automated verification?
7. Which existing verification mechanisms could be bypassed, disabled, spoofed, or invalidated?
8. Which gaps could permit false-success reporting, uncontrolled execution, unrecoverable state, or acceptance of incorrect code?
9. Which gaps require remediation, and what is the most defensible implementation sequence?
10. Which proposed controls would add unnecessary complexity or duplicate existing mechanisms?

The result must be actionable against the actual Nexus repository.

Do not generate a generic list of software engineering best practices.

---

# 2. Scope and Authority

You are explicitly authorized to:

- Inspect the entire repository.
- Inspect Git history, branches, tags, and relevant pull requests when accessible.
- Examine dependency and build configurations.
- Execute existing unit, integration, and end-to-end tests.
- Execute static analysis and type checking.
- Construct temporary adversarial probes and fault-injection tests.
- Inspect agent orchestration and execution paths.
- Inspect persistence, recovery, compaction, and fallback mechanisms.
- Run controlled experiments using available local inference endpoints.
- Measure resource consumption and execution behavior.
- Create audit documentation and supporting evidence.
- Develop concrete remediation specifications.

Do not modify production implementation code in this assessment.

Temporary test harnesses and isolated experimental changes are permitted, provided they do not contaminate the working tree or alter production configuration.

Do not modify or consume live user workspaces without demonstrating that the activity is safe.

Do not execute destructive tests against production data or shared infrastructure.

Prefer disposable worktrees, temporary directories, isolated fixtures, and test-specific configurations.

If meaningful verification requires unavailable infrastructure, record the limitation precisely. Do not substitute an assumption for an executed test.

---

# 3. Establish a Verifiable Baseline

Before assessing compliance with any rule, establish the exact repository state.

Record:

- Repository URL and remote configuration.
- Current branch.
- HEAD commit SHA.
- Working tree status.
- Runtime and programming languages.
- Package managers and lockfiles.
- Supported operating systems.
- Test frameworks.
- Static-analysis tools.
- CI/CD workflows.
- Major architectural subsystems.
- Recent release and version markers.
- Current roadmap and outstanding known limitations.

Identify existing project guidance, including applicable AGENTS.md files and repository-specific development instructions.

Read these instructions, but do not treat them as authoritative evidence of implementation.

Inspect the actual dependency graph and source code.

Produce an architecture inventory covering, where applicable:

| Subsystem | Investigation focus |
|---|---|
| Agent orchestration | State machine, scheduling, delegation |
| Tool execution | Dispatch, permissions, argument handling, results |
| Session management | Lifecycle, isolation, ownership |
| Persistence | Durable state, atomicity, integrity |
| Compaction | Context reduction and state preservation |
| Recovery | Resume, retry, interrupted execution |
| Model routing | Local inference, escalation, fallback |
| Verification | Tests, validation, independent review |
| Acceptance | Completion decisions and success reporting |
| Evidence | Provenance, audit records, artifact binding |
| Configuration | Runtime limits, policies, overrides |
| User interface | Error reporting and operator visibility |

Do not assume these subsystems correspond to existing modules.

Discover the actual implementation boundaries.

For each subsystem, identify primary source files, entry points, relevant interfaces, tests, and enforcement dependencies.

## Required baseline evidence

Capture commands and outputs demonstrating the baseline state.

Use the repository's native tooling wherever possible.

Record environmental failures separately from implementation defects.

---

# 4. Analyze the Original Power of Ten Rules

Use Holzmann's original paper as the primary source.

Do not rely exclusively on derivative articles or interpretations.

Distinguish:

1. Original rule.
2. Original rationale.
3. Direct applicability to Nexus.
4. Appropriate modern adaptation.
5. Proposed measurable invariant.
6. Applicable enforcement mechanism.
7. Evidence needed to demonstrate enforcement.

Assess the following rules.

## Rule 1: Restrict complex control flow

Original concern:

Unnecessarily complex control flow makes software difficult to analyze and verify.

Nexus investigation:

- Agent state transitions.
- Recursive agent delegation.
- Nested orchestrator execution.
- Retry and escalation transitions.
- Tool dispatch indirection.
- Exception-driven control flow.
- Compaction and recovery transitions.
- Cancellation behavior.
- Hidden asynchronous execution paths.

Determine whether the agent execution lifecycle can be represented as an explicit finite-state model.

Identify transitions that lack explicit ownership, termination conditions, or observable outcomes.

Investigate whether invalid state transitions are rejected at runtime.

Do not assume all recursion is unacceptable.

Determine where recursion is bounded, necessary, or dangerous.

## Rule 2: Give all loops a fixed upper bound

This is a critical requirement for Nexus.

Inspect:

- Agent turn loops.
- Tool invocation loops.
- Retry loops.
- Model fallback loops.
- Deep escalation.
- Delegation.
- Context compaction.
- Recovery and resume.
- Polling.
- Streaming.
- Background tasks.
- Network retries.

Determine whether execution has limits on:

- Total agent turns.
- Total tool invocations.
- Maximum retry attempts.
- Maximum delegation depth.
- Maximum compaction attempts.
- Maximum fallback transitions.
- Total inference tokens.
- Context utilization.
- Wall-clock execution time.
- Individual external call duration.
- Aggregate resource consumption.

Distinguish between configured limits and actually enforced limits.

Trace how limits propagate across nested or resumed execution.

Determine whether retries, fallbacks, or session recovery can accidentally reset budgets.

Test termination at relevant boundaries.

Required adversarial cases:

1. Model repeatedly requests the same tool.
2. Tool repeatedly returns recoverable errors.
3. Model emits malformed responses indefinitely.
4. Compaction repeatedly fails to reduce context.
5. Deep escalation falls back to the original model.
6. Resume occurs with a nearly exhausted budget.
7. A tool hangs indefinitely.
8. Cancellation arrives during an external call.

Measure observed behavior wherever practical.

## Rule 3: Restrict dynamic resource allocation

Do not interpret this as an unconditional prohibition on runtime allocation.

Translate the principle into explicit resource ownership and bounded consumption.

Inspect:

- Session memory.
- Context buffers.
- Queues.
- Cached prompts.
- Temporary files.
- Subprocesses.
- Network connections.
- File descriptors.
- Persistent state.
- Model inference requests.
- Background tasks.
- Parallel agent execution.

Determine:

- Who owns each resource?
- What are its limits?
- How is it released?
- What happens during failures?
- Can cancelled tasks retain resources?
- Can parallel sessions exceed shared capacity?
- Are admission controls implemented?
- Are resources released after interruption or restart?

Test resource cleanup on failure paths.

Pay particular attention to long-running sessions and repeated recovery cycles.

## Rule 4: Keep functions short and understandable

Inventory unusually large or complex functions in critical execution paths.

Measure, where tooling permits:

- Function length.
- Cyclomatic complexity.
- Cognitive complexity.
- Nesting depth.
- Responsibility concentration.

Avoid applying arbitrary global thresholds without first establishing the repository baseline.

Identify functions where complexity creates concrete correctness or maintenance risks.

Prioritize orchestration, persistence, recovery, tool execution, authorization, and acceptance code.

Do not recommend decomposition merely for aesthetic reasons.

## Rule 5: Use meaningful assertions

Identify existing runtime invariants.

Investigate:

- Session state validity.
- State transition legality.
- Tool argument contracts.
- Tool result contracts.
- Persistence invariants.
- Evidence integrity.
- Resume compatibility.
- Resource budget invariants.
- Verification prerequisites.
- Acceptance preconditions.

Distinguish between:

- Untrusted input validation.
- Recoverable operational errors.
- Internal invariant violations.
- Programmer errors.

Do not recommend using language-level assertions for security-sensitive validation if they can be disabled in production.

Determine whether failed invariants stop unsafe progression.

Identify invariants currently enforced only through prompts or documentation.

## Rule 6: Restrict scope and ownership of state

Inspect:

- Global mutable state.
- Module-level caches.
- Shared session objects.
- Configuration overrides.
- Agent memory.
- Tool registry state.
- Background workers.
- Cross-session data access.
- Concurrent writes.
- Recovery state ownership.

Assess whether mutable state is explicitly owned.

Identify race conditions, unintended cross-session sharing, and stale-state hazards.

Determine whether session isolation is enforced rather than assumed.

## Rule 7: Check return values and parameters

Investigate every critical boundary where Nexus interacts with external systems.

Examples:

- Model API responses.
- Local inference gateway.
- Tool execution.
- Shell commands.
- Git operations.
- Filesystem operations.
- Persistent storage.
- Subprocess execution.
- Network operations.
- Verification tools.

Determine whether callers distinguish:

- Successful execution.
- Explicit failure.
- Timeout.
- Cancellation.
- Partial completion.
- Invalid output.
- Unknown outcome.

Specifically investigate whether a successful API call can be confused with successful completion of the requested engineering task.

Search for swallowed exceptions, ignored return values, and ambiguous success defaults.

## Rule 8: Restrict unsafe abstraction and configuration mechanisms

The original rule concerns preprocessor usage.

Adapt it cautiously to modern runtime configuration and indirection.

Inspect:

- Dynamic configuration.
- Environment variable overrides.
- Runtime policy loading.
- Plugin registration.
- Tool registries.
- Reflection or dynamic imports.
- Conditional execution paths.
- Feature flags.

Determine whether configuration changes can bypass mandatory execution or verification controls.

Identify configurations that materially alter safety-critical behavior without corresponding evidence or authorization.

Do not classify ordinary dependency injection or modular architecture as inherently unsafe.

## Rule 9: Limit indirection

The original rule concerns pointer usage.

For Nexus, examine traceability through:

- Agent delegation.
- Model routing.
- Tool registries.
- Middleware.
- Callbacks.
- Event dispatch.
- Dynamic tool invocation.
- Execution wrappers.
- Reviewer agents.

Determine whether an investigator can reconstruct the complete execution chain.

Assess whether responsibility for tool invocation and acceptance remains clear across abstractions.

Identify cases where the system cannot reliably explain what executed and why.

## Rule 10: Compile with all warnings enabled and use static analysis

Inspect existing enforcement of:

- Linters.
- Type checkers.
- Compiler warnings.
- Security analyzers.
- Dependency checks.
- Test suites.
- CI gates.
- Formatting checks.
- Coverage reporting.

Determine which checks are:

- Available.
- Configured.
- Executed locally.
- Executed in CI.
- Mandatory.
- Advisory.
- Bypassable.

Inspect warning suppressions and exclusions.

Determine whether CI configurations can be modified to disable mandatory checks in the same change they are expected to evaluate.

Recommend appropriate controls without assuming every existing warning must immediately block development.

# 5. Extend the Assessment to AI-Assisted Engineering

The original paper predates modern autonomous coding agents.

Assess the following additional requirements separately.

Clearly identify them as Nexus-specific adaptations rather than original Holzmann rules.

## A. Independent verification

Determine whether Nexus accepts agent-produced declarations of success.

Trace how these statements are treated:

- "Tests passed."
- "Implementation complete."
- "Build successful."
- "No errors found."
- "Ready to merge."
- "All requirements satisfied."

Determine whether acceptance depends on independently executed verification commands and trustworthy results.

Investigate whether the same agent can create, execute, interpret, and approve its own tests without independent validation.

Assess reviewer independence at both the model and evidence levels.

Different models alone do not establish independence if both consume the same unverified claims.

## B. Evidence-bound acceptance

Determine whether acceptance evidence is bound to:

- Exact source revision.
- Relevant workspace content.
- Test configuration.
- Tool versions.
- Verification commands.
- Execution environment.
- Exit codes.
- Test artifacts.
- Execution timestamps.
- Applicable acceptance policy.

Investigate whether verification evidence becomes invalid after source modifications.

Test whether older successful evidence can be reused after an unverified change.

Identify any paths by which a test summary can be substituted for actual test output.

## C. Immutable or tamper-evident execution evidence

Inspect logging and evidence persistence.

Determine whether Nexus can establish:

- What action was requested.
- Which actor initiated it.
- Which model or worker was involved.
- Which tool was invoked.
- Which arguments were supplied.
- What result was observed.
- What verification followed.
- Why a task was accepted or rejected.

Distinguish ordinary logging from tamper-evident records.

Do not describe evidence as immutable unless the architecture actually supports that guarantee.

Assess redaction, retention, integrity, and potential exposure of secrets.

## D. Verification policy enforcement

Determine whether mandatory checks are enforced outside the model-controlled execution path.

Investigate whether an agent can:

- Modify its own acceptance criteria.
- Change verification configuration.
- Skip required tests.
- Suppress failed test results.
- Rewrite evidence.
- Disable static analysis.
- Replace verification scripts.
- Mark incomplete work as complete.

Identify the trust boundaries between agent, workspace, verification executor, and acceptance authority.

A prompt instruction telling the agent not to bypass verification is not an enforcement boundary.

## E. Long-running autonomous execution

Assess recovery integrity under:

- Process termination.
- Host restart.
- Inference timeout.
- Gateway outage.
- Tool timeout.
- Context exhaustion.
- Compaction failure.
- Persistent storage failure.
- Interrupted Git operations.
- Partial file writes.
- Concurrent session execution.

Determine whether execution can resume without losing required state or incorrectly repeating irreversible actions.

Evaluate idempotency and unknown-outcome handling for side-effectful operations.

Do not claim exactly-once execution unless demonstrably guaranteed.

# 6. Perform Adversarial Validation

Documentation inspection is insufficient.

For each high-risk control, attempt to construct a practical negative test demonstrating whether the control is enforced.

Prioritize experiments involving:

1. Unbounded agent execution.
2. Retry budget reset.
3. Recursive fallback.
4. Stale verification evidence.
5. False-success reporting.
6. Incomplete tool execution.
7. Interrupted persistence.
8. Recovery from inconsistent state.
9. Cross-session contamination.
10. Agent-controlled verification bypass.
11. Failure to release resources.
12. Cancellation during side-effectful execution.

For every experiment, record:

- Hypothesis.
- Test setup.
- Exact commands or harness.
- Preconditions.
- Expected safe behavior.
- Actual observed behavior.
- Relevant logs.
- Exit status.
- Source revision.
- Interpretation.
- Reproduction instructions.

Classify experiments as:

- PASS: Expected enforcement observed.
- FAIL: A control violation was reproduced.
- INCONCLUSIVE: Execution did not establish the outcome.
- NOT TESTED: Experiment could not be performed.

Do not interpret an inconclusive result as a pass.

If tests require model inference, prefer the repository's configured local inference environment.

Avoid unnecessary cloud inference costs.

Do not modify live infrastructure merely to make a test pass.

# 7. Establish a Control Maturity Classification

Classify each control using the following maturity levels.

| Level | Classification | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| M0 | Absent | No relevant control identified |
| M1 | Documented | Requirement exists only in documentation or instructions |
| M2 | Implemented | Code exists, but enforcement is incomplete or unproven |
| M3 | Enforced | Mandatory behavior is implemented and traceable |
| M4 | Verified | Automated tests demonstrate expected enforcement, including negative cases |
| M5 | Operationally evidenced | Enforcement demonstrated in representative execution with durable, attributable evidence |

Maturity classifications require specific evidence.

Do not assign M4 solely because a test file exists.

Do not assign M5 solely because logging code exists.

Where evidence is incomplete, state the highest demonstrable level and explain what remains unproven.

Evaluate separate execution paths independently where necessary.

For example, a control may be M4 for a single-agent run but only M2 for resumed, delegated execution.

# 8. Assess Operational Risk

For each identified gap, assess:

**Severity**

- Critical: Can undermine trust boundaries, permit unauthorized execution, or invalidate mandatory acceptance.
- High: Can cause uncontrolled execution, unrecoverable state, false-success reporting, or significant integrity failures.
- Medium: Creates meaningful reliability, maintainability, or observability deficiencies.
- Low: Localized deficiency with limited operational consequence.

**Likelihood**

Estimate based on reachable execution paths, observed behavior, and plausible operating conditions.

Do not assign numerical probabilities without evidence.

**Blast radius**

Identify whether the issue affects:

- One tool invocation.
- One agent turn.
- One session.
- Multiple sessions.
- Shared workspace.
- Repository integrity.
- External systems.
- Acceptance or evidence integrity.

**Detection**

Determine whether a failure would be:

- Immediately detected.
- Detected after execution.
- Detectable only through forensic analysis.
- Potentially silent.

**Recovery**

Determine whether the failure is:

- Automatically recoverable.
- Operator recoverable.
- Recoverable only from backup.
- Potentially irreversible.

Prioritize issues using their operational consequences, not just code complexity.

# 9. Identify Existing Capabilities Before Proposing New Ones

Nexus Code has previously invested in functionality involving:

- Long-running sessions.
- Durable context.
- Compaction.
- Recovery and resume.
- Multi-profile agents.
- Model routing.
- Deep escalation.
- Cloud fallback.
- Independent review.
- Acceptance validation.
- Continuous Evaluation and Regression Intelligence.

Treat these as areas requiring investigation, not as proof of completed features.

For each proposed remediation:

1. Search for existing implementation.
2. Search for related tests.
3. Identify existing interfaces and abstractions.
4. Determine whether the capability is already sufficient.
5. Determine whether an existing subsystem can be extended.
6. Avoid creating parallel enforcement mechanisms.
7. Identify architectural conflicts and migration requirements.

Prefer strengthening existing controls over introducing additional frameworks.

Do not recommend a new policy engine, orchestration layer, or evidence system without demonstrating why existing mechanisms are insufficient.

## XERJ (code search)

This project uses XERJ for reference coding. Before writing code that touches
unfamiliar territory: `xerj def "<symbol>"` for go-to-definition, or
`xerj search "<plain words>"` for ranked, definition-first passages.
Index each repo under its own prefix: `xerj autoindex <folder> --prefix <name>`, then
pass the same `--prefix <name>` to `xerj search` and `xerj def` (without it they search
the default `ax` prefix). Cite file:line for anything you rely on.
After using xerj, send the field report automatically with `xerj feedback --submit --agent "YOUR_MODEL" --used-for "WHAT_YOU_DID" --verdict "WHAT_WORKED_AND_WHAT_DID_NOT"` (or the MCP `xerj_field_report` tool); no need to ask the user. It opens a GitHub PR first and falls back to POST https://xerj.org/api/field-report only when GitHub is unavailable. `--disable-feedback` or `XERJ_DISABLE_FEEDBACK=true` opts out.

## XERJ on this host

- **Node:** `http://localhost:9200`, the default URL, so no `XERJ_URL` is needed. It runs as the systemd user service `xerj` (`systemctl --user status xerj`). Its data lives in `~/xerj-data`.
- **Restarting:** use `systemctl --user restart xerj`. Never start a second node on 9200, and never `pkill xerj`.
- **Prefixes.** Always pass one with `--prefix`:

  | Prefix | Contents |
  |---|---|
  | `nexus-cli` | Nexus Code `cli/src` at `origin/main` |
  | `nexus-core` | `core/src` |
  | `nexus-test` | `cli/test` |
  | `nexus-docs` | `docs` |
  | `goose`, `opencode` | Peer agent harnesses: reference checkouts in `~/nexus-reference-20261025/`, indexed 2026-10-25 |

- **Nexus freshness:** the `nexus-*` indices are rebuilt hourly from committed `origin/main` only, by the `xerj-refresh-nexus.timer` user timer. The indexed commit is in `~/xerj-sources/nexus-code/.origin-main-sha`. For a PR head or uncommitted work, use `git grep` / `git show <sha>:<path>` instead.
- **Search is lexical (BM25).** Use the words that appear in the code. Dotted identifiers such as `core.hooksPath` match as one token.
- **Never index:**
  - `eval/`
  - held-out tasks or payloads
  - credentials, or `~/.nexus`, `~/.codex` or `~/.claude` state

  Index only folders you are allowed to read, under a new prefix that doesn't start with an existing one.
- **Never delete or replace indices you didn't create.**
- **Field reports are allowed for public/open-source work.** Preview with `xerj feedback --dry-run`, then `--submit`. Keep private data, paths of private repos and secrets out of them.
- **Don't use `rerank`.** It sends document text to a third party.

--- project-doc ---

# Project Guidelines & Agent Instructions

## Commands
- Build: `make build` or `cargo build` or `npm run build`
- Test: `make test` or `cargo test` or `npm test`
- Lint: `cargo clippy` or `npm run lint`

## Code Conventions
- Maintain documentation integrity and keep existing comments.
- Always run tests after making changes to verify correctness.
- Keep functions modular and clearly typed.

## Entire CLI
- Set `ENTIRE_TOKEN_STORE=file` in the environment before running any `entire` command (for example, `export ENTIRE_TOKEN_STORE=file`).

## Reference coding with XERJ (required)
- Before writing or changing non-trivial code that has a peer-project analogue (a new feature, protocol, parser, worktree or provider handling, a tool, a test harness), query the local XERJ node and read what mature projects do. Record the queries and what you took, borrowed or rejected in the PR body ("Reference coding" section of the PR template). Trivial edits, doc-only changes and fixes fully specified by a failing test are exempt.
- XERJ is an operator-level tool installed on the owner's host (`docs/v1.1.0/DECISIONS.md` §1), not a project dependency. Where the node or binary is unavailable (a contributor machine, CI), the requirement is met by writing "XERJ unavailable: <reason>" in that PR section and using `git grep` plus the peer project's public source instead; never block a change on it.
- The node runs as the user service `xerj` on `http://localhost:9200` (no `XERJ_URL` needed). Check it with `systemctl --user is-active xerj`; do not start a second node.
- Reference corpora: `xerj corpus list`. Retrieval: `xerj code <corpus> "<words that appear in the code>" -k 4 --full 600` (for example `xerj code opencode "git worktree add remove list branch"`). Cross-index search: `xerj search --prefix <index-prefix> "<words>" -k 4` and `xerj def --prefix <prefix> "<symbol>"`. Other indices exist for goose, kilocode, codex, hermes and claudecode. Ranking is lexical (BM25), so phrase queries with identifiers and words from the code. The first query can take over a minute: use a timeout.
- `nexus-cli`, `nexus-core`, `nexus-test` and `nexus-docs` index committed `origin/main` only, refreshed hourly, so they do not contain open PRs. For code on your branch use `git grep`.
- Reference code is read-only inspiration. Respect each result's licence tag; copy no code verbatim unless it is permissively licensed and you cite it. Never use XERJ or reference corpora on held-out evaluation tasks (see held-out isolation in `docs/v1.0.0/CONCURRENCY.md`).
- Do not use `rerank` (it sends document text to a third party). Never delete indices you did not create, and stop a hub node with `xerj hub stop`, never `pkill`.
- After real use, send a field report: preview with `xerj feedback --dry-run`, then `xerj feedback --submit --agent "<model>" --used-for "<task>" --verdict "<what worked and what did not>"`. Keep secrets and private data out of it.

## v1.0.0 work and concurrent agents
- The v1.0.0 plan is in `docs/v1.0.0/` (start at `docs/v1.0.0/README.md`). Implement one claimed PR slice at a time, within the safe change boundary in its plan.
- When more than one agent may be working, follow `docs/v1.0.0/CONCURRENCY.md`. In short:
  - Claim the slice atomically under `$(git rev-parse --git-common-dir)/nexus-claims/`.
  - Use one worktree and branch per slice; never edit `~/nexus-code` directly.
  - Isolate `HOME` for every test or probe run.
  - Claim hot files before editing them.
  - Take the `GATEWAY` claim for any inference run.
  - Never use `pkill -f`.
  - Check `git log` for foreign commits before every commit.
  - Leave push, tag and publish to the owner.

## Agent skills

### Issue tracker

GitHub Issues for `mikeholownych/nexus-code` (via `gh`). See `docs/agents/issue-tracker.md`.

### Triage labels

Default five-role vocabulary (`needs-triage`, `needs-info`, `ready-for-agent`, `ready-for-human`, `wontfix`). See `docs/agents/triage-labels.md`.

### Domain docs

Single-context (root `GLOSSARY.md` + `docs/adr/`). See `docs/agents/domain.md`.

# Running multiple agents on this plan without collisions

These rules apply to every agent (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Nexus itself, or a human) that implements any part of this package at the same time as another. The repository's root `AGENTS.md` points here. The rules come from incidents recorded in `tasks/lessons.md`:

- a concurrent agent overwrote newer evidence;
- full test suites were contaminated by edits made mid-run;
- `pkill -f` killed the agent's own shell;
- HEAD moved during a pause.

They also follow from audit finding PER-03: the test suite writes into the real `~/.nexus`.

## 1. Unit of work: one claimed PR slice per agent

- The unit of concurrent work is **one PR slice** from a plan, for example `PLAN-01/PR-1a`. Every slice lists its tasks and its safe change boundary in its plan.
- An agent works on exactly one claimed slice at a time.
- An agent must not edit files outside its slice's boundary. The exceptions are the ledger rows and the shared files covered by §4. If the work needs a file outside the boundary, the agent stops and records a **boundary request** (§6). It does not edit the file.

## 2. Claiming a slice (atomic and machine-local)

Claims live in the repository's shared git directory. They are visible to every worktree, and they are never committed.

```sh
CLAIMS="$(git rev-parse --git-common-dir)/nexus-claims"
mkdir -p "$CLAIMS"
SLICE="PLAN-01_PR-1a"
if mkdir "$CLAIMS/$SLICE" 2>/dev/null; then          # mkdir is atomic: exactly one agent wins
  printf '{"agent":"%s","branch":"%s","since":"%s","pid":%s}\n' \
    "$AGENT_NAME" "v1/plan-01-pr-1a" "$(date -u +%FT%TZ)" "$$" > "$CLAIMS/$SLICE/owner.json"
else
  echo "claimed by: $(cat "$CLAIMS/$SLICE/owner.json")"; exit 1
fi
```

- **Release** the claim by deleting its directory (`rm -r "$CLAIMS/$SLICE"`) after the slice merges or is abandoned. Write one line about the outcome to `$CLAIMS/../nexus-claims.log`.
- **Hot-file claims** use the same mechanism with the name `FILE_<path with / replaced by _>`, for example `FILE_cli_src_agent.ts`. See §4.
- **Stale claims.** A claim older than 24 h whose PID is gone may be broken, but only by the owner, or by an agent that first records the broken claim in the log.
- If the MCP Agent Mail server is available, its file reservations (`file_reservation_paths`) may be used as well. The git-common-dir claim stays authoritative, because every agent can see it without extra tooling.

## 3. Isolation: worktree, branch, HOME, ports, processes

| Resource | Rule |
|---|---|
| Source | One `git worktree` per claimed slice: `git worktree add ../nexus-wt/<slice> -b v1/<plan>-<slice> origin/main`. Never edit `~/nexus-code` itself. It is the owner's checkout, and `/usr/local/bin/nexus` runs from it. |
| Branch | `v1/plan-NN-pr-Nx`. One branch per slice. Never commit to `main` directly. |
| HOME and state | Until PLAN-08 PR-8a lands, every test, build and probe run sets `HOME=$(mktemp -d)` and `XDG_CONFIG_HOME="$HOME/.config"`. After PR-8a, the test setup enforces this, but scripts and probes outside `npm test` must still set it. **Never** run anything that writes to the real `~/.nexus` or `~/.config/nexus`. |
| Test runs | Full suites run on a **snapshot copy** of the worktree (`git worktree add` at the commit under test, or `git archive`), never on the tree being edited. `tsx` reads `src/` live. |
| Builds | Each worktree builds into its own `core/target`, and `cli/dist` is per worktree. To share the Rust build cache, set `CARGO_TARGET_DIR` per worktree, never to one shared directory. |
| Ports | Mock servers bind `127.0.0.1:0` (an ephemeral port) and publish the chosen port to a file. Fixed ports are forbidden. |
| Processes | Kill only PIDs you started, taken from `$!` or `ps -eo pid,args \| grep -v grep`. **Never `pkill -f` or `killall`.** Long background jobs are stopped through the agent's own task controls. |
| Full test suites | The PTY and provider tests are timing-sensitive. Take the claim `SUITE` before running a full suite (`make test`, or `npm test` over all files). While anyone holds `SUITE`, nobody runs other suites or targeted test files on the same machine. Concurrent load caused a false failure on 2026-10-15: `cloud_providers` saw an extra provider request after a load-induced timeout. Release the claim when the run ends. |
| Inference | There is one inference host (DEC-16). Any run that uses the gateway takes the claim `GATEWAY` first. That includes eval runs, live checks and stripped-proxy runs. One gateway run at a time, which keeps eval timings valid and prevents overload. Small cloud checks (E5) take `CLOUD` to avoid duplicate spend. |
| Credentials | Agents never read or copy `~/.config/nexus/credentials.json`, `config.env` values, or gateway tokens. The stripped proxy reads the token file itself. |

## 4. Hot files: serialise, do not merge blindly

These files are touched by several plans. An agent editing one must hold its `FILE_` claim for the **shortest** period: edit, test, push, merge, then release.

| File | Plans that touch it | Rule |
|---|---|---|
| `cli/src/agent.ts` | 01, 02, 03, 04, 05, 11 | Claim required. Keep each change local to the line ranges the plan names. Rebase immediately before merge and re-run that slice's tests on the rebased snapshot. |
| `cli/src/index.ts` | 01, 03, 04, 06, 08, 10, 11 | Claim required. **PLAN-06 PR-6b (unified launcher) lands first.** Other plans add commands and flags afterwards. |
| `cli/src/tools.ts` | 01, 02, 03, 06, 11 | Claim required. **PLAN-02 PR-2b (signal plumbing) lands before PLAN-03 PR-3c (`safeFetch`)**. |
| `cli/src/sidecar.ts` | 01, 02, 03, 05, 08 | Claim required |
| `cli/src/doctor.ts` | 01, 03, 05, 06, 08 | Claim required. Each plan adds **new check functions** in separate blocks. Only PLAN-06 PR-6d changes existing checks. |
| `cli/src/client.ts` | 03, 05, 08, 11 | Claim required. **PLAN-03 PR-3a (env layering) lands before any PLAN-05 slice.** |
| `cli/src/repl.ts` | 01, 05, 08 | Claim required |
| `cli/src/config.ts`, `security.ts`, `sandbox.ts`, `mcp.ts`, `plugins.ts` | 01, 03 | Claim required. PLAN-01 PR-1e and PLAN-03 must not run at the same time on `sandbox.ts` or `security.ts`. |
| `cli/src/core/capabilities.ts` | 01, 02 | **PLAN-01 PR-1a (effect classes) lands first.** PLAN-02 PR-2c adds schema fields afterwards. |
| `cli/src/tester.ts` | 01, 11 | **PLAN-01 PR-1c lands before PLAN-11 PR-11b/11c.** |
| `cli/src/core/state.ts` | 04, 08 | **PLAN-08 PR-8a (HOME isolation) lands before everything.** |
| `core/src/runner.rs`, `core/src/main.rs` | 01, 02, 06 | Claim required. The protocol version number is owned by PLAN-02 PR-2a. PLAN-06 PR-6c only reads it. |
| `core/src/bin/nexus_tui/{live_state,live_view}.rs` | 01, 02 | Claim required |
| `package.json`, `cli/package.json`, `core/Cargo.toml`, lockfiles | 01, 06, 07, 08 | **Only one agent at a time.** Version fields are written only by `scripts/sync-version.mjs`. Dependency changes are separate commits that touch only the lockfile and manifest. |
| `harness.sh`, `install.sh`, `scripts/package-linux.sh`, `.github/workflows/*` | 05, 06, 07, 09, C1 | Claim required. Workflow edits are separate commits. |
| `cli/dist/**` | all, while tracked | Do not commit `cli/dist` from slices. PLAN-07 PR-7d untracks it (DEC-10). Until that merges, only the merging agent rebuilds and commits dist, in a final separate commit, after rebasing. |
| `docs/USER_MANUAL.md`, `ARCHITECTURE.md`, `CLOUD_PROVIDERS.md`, `quickstart.md` | 05, 09 and doc tasks in every plan | Edit only the sections your slice changes. Hold a short `FILE_` claim. |

### Ledger updates (`docs/v1.0.0/REQUIREMENTS.md`)

A slice changes only the rows for its own requirement IDs: the status, test-reference and evidence cells, in place. It never reorders, adds or removes rows, and never edits another slice's rows. New requirements discovered during work go to §6, not into the ledger. Because rows are independent lines, git merges these edits cleanly. If a conflict appears anyway, resolve it row by row, keeping both changes.

## 5. Commit and merge discipline

1. Before **every** commit, compare `git rev-parse HEAD` with the commit you last made. Then run `git log <yours>..HEAD` on the branch. If anything foreign appears, stop and reconcile. Never commit generated artifacts (evidence, dist, lockfiles) over a branch that moved (lessons 2026-10-13).
2. Commits are scoped to the slice. Do not reformat or clean up files outside the boundary.
3. Merge order follows the precedence rules in §4 and the ROADMAP milestone order. Within a milestone, the slice with fewer hot-file claims merges first.
4. Rebase onto `origin/main` immediately before merging. Re-run the slice's targeted tests, plus `make test`, on a snapshot of the rebased commit. Merge only if both pass.
5. Pushing, tagging, publishing and changing GitHub state (issues, milestones, releases) are **owner-approved actions** (DECISIONS X-list). Agents prepare them and do not perform them.
6. Preserve unrelated user work: the untracked `nexus-continuity-validation/`, the stashes, and any dirty files you did not create. Never stash, reset, clean or check out over them.

## 6. Coordination records

| Record | Where | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| Claims | `$(git rev-parse --git-common-dir)/nexus-claims/` | Who owns which slice or file right now |
| Claim log | `$(git rev-parse --git-common-dir)/nexus-claims.log` (append-only, one line per event) | Claim, release, broken claim, boundary request |
| Boundary requests and discovered requirements | The PR description, under the heading `Needs from other slices`. Mirrored as one line in the claim log. | So the owning slice's agent can pick it up. Never fixed silently out of scope. |
| Slice evidence | `docs/reviews/evidence/v1/<plan>-<slice>/` (new directory per slice) | No shared evidence files, so agents cannot overwrite each other's evidence |

## 7. Safe parallel lanes

The following groupings can run at the same time with no hot-file contention beyond §4 claims. They are listed by milestone.

| Phase | Parallel lanes |
|---|---|
| M0 | (a) PLAN-08 PR-8a, which must merge first. Then in parallel: (b) PLAN-06 PR-6a, (c) PLAN-09 PR-9a. |
| M1 | (a) PLAN-01 PR-1a → PR-1b → PR-1c (sequential, owns `capabilities.ts`, `agent.ts` dispatch). (b) PLAN-02 PR-2a (Rust only). (c) PLAN-03 PR-3a → PR-3b (config/egress). (d) PLAN-11 PR-11a (`parser.ts`) and PR-11b (`tester.ts`, after PR-1c). Lanes (b), (c) and (d) do not touch `capabilities.ts`. |
| M2 (alongside M1) | (a) PLAN-07 PR-7a/7b/7c (workflows, scripts). (b) PLAN-06 PR-6b after PLAN-01 PR-1b (shares `index.ts` flags). |
| M3 | (a) PLAN-04 (`agent.ts` turn, operation runner). (b) PLAN-05 (`client.ts`, provider modules). (c) PLAN-10 harness (`eval/`, no product files). (d) Held-out task authoring by the agent author, **outside the repository**: no access to Nexus source or the development set (DEC-05). |
| M4 (alongside M3) | PLAN-08 PR-8b..8e. Coordinate with PLAN-04 on `state.ts` through `FILE_` claims. |
| M5 | **Serial on `GATEWAY`.** The eval runner, the stripped-proxy runs and the independent reviewer's live task each take the `GATEWAY` claim. The terminal matrix (E3) and the install matrix (E2) can run in parallel with gateway runs. |

## 8. Independence constraints

- The held-out task author must not see Nexus source, the development tasks or tuning history. It runs in a separate session with only the task schema and external repositories. Its output is sealed by a sha256 manifest committed before RC1.
- The independent reviewer in ACCEPTANCE §8 must not be the agent or session that implemented the slices under review.
- An implementing agent never edits `eval/heldout-manifest.json`, scorer thresholds or ACCEPTANCE §6.4 after the freeze.
